en: Auspiciousness.
The Sāṅkhyakārikā with the Māṭharavṛtti [salutes] the eternal creator of all sciences, who dwells in the sun.
I have been born through supreme devotion to the Lord, the Light of Kapila.
Homage to that Kapila, by whom, out of compassion for the world submerged in the ocean of ignorance, a boat consisting of Sāṃkhya was fashioned here for the purpose of crossing over. // 2 //
Having paid homage to him, I shall declare the cause of that knowledge for the benefit of all disciples, as a concise compendium of few words. (3)

Because of the assault of the threefold suffering, there arises a desire to know the means for its removal. If it is argued that such inquiry is useless because a remedy is already seen in the world, we say no, because that remedy is neither certain nor final. (ISk 1)
The introduction to this noble work is now set forth:
"The location, the cause, the speaker, the listener, the purpose of the listener,
and the statement of the connection and so forth— this is called the introduction."
For here, the Blessed One, the Great Sage, endowed with innate virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty,
was born as the incarnation of the Blessed Ancient Puruṣa out of a desire to favor the world; he became known as Kapila, the son of Prajāpati Kardama, by Devahūtī, the daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu.

By means of that knowledge, which consists in the perception of the distinction between the qualities (guṇas) and the Puruṣa, he desired to show the shoreless the further shore—as if by a hand to hold;
as if by the moon-nectar for the world bitten by the serpent of Time; and as if by the perfect medicine for the removal of the incurable disease of worldly existence (bhava).

Endowed with this awakening— which was like a lamp for utterly destroying the darkness of ignorance and like an axe for felling the tree of delusion that obstructs the path to liberation— he beheld this world sinking into blind darkness.
Upon seeing it, compassion arose within him.
"Alas! This world, bound by beginningless time, exists by its very nature in blinding darkness.
Then that great yogi, having conceived compassion—thinking, "How may I bring about the grace of this wretched universe dwelling in blinding darkness?"—fell into reflection in his mind.
While reflecting thus, he [perceived] a distinguished Brāhmaṇa of the Āsuri lineage, a performer of sacrifices for a thousand years, who was [fit to be] an initiate.
Having understood this through the knowledge of the instruction on Brahman, he became free from sloth and spoke these words: "O Āsuri, do you take delight in the dharma of a householder?
He replied to him: "I do take delight, sir."
Having been addressed thus, the sage, concluding that "this man's discernment and dispassion are only slightly developed," departed;
then, when a second thousand years had passed, he returned and spoke to him in the same manner: "O Āsuri, do you still take delight in the dharma of a householder?"
He said to him, "I am enjoying it, sir.
Then that great lord of yogins, having departed in the same manner, returned when the third thousand years were complete and said, "O Āsuri, do you take pleasure in the dharma of a householder?
He replied to him, "I do not take pleasure in it, sir."
Then he was asked by the Blessed One: "How so?
Āsuri replied again: "Because of the assault of the threefold suffering.
Then Kapila said: "Dear one, if you are able to dwell in the life of celibacy, then we shall teach you the remedy for these three types of suffering."
He replied, "Venerable sir, indeed I am able to follow the command of the Blessed Ones.
Having thus abandoned the dharma of a householder, as well as his sons, wife, and other attachments,
he went forth as a renunciant under the venerable Kapilācārya, the yogin.
He became a disciple.
In that regard, if someone were to ask, "From where did his desire to know arise, by which he approached the teacher's household?"—
to this, the following is the reply.
From the affliction by the threefold suffering, the desire to know has arisen:
what is the supreme here,
and what is the true nature?
Thinking, "What is the supreme good?
By doing what shall I have accomplished my purpose?", he approached the teacher's house. For it is said:
"That is true austerity, that is true recitation, that is true concentration, that is true knowledge, and that is true scholarship."
So that there may never again be a falling back into the ocean of saṃsāra.
Thus it is heard.
Furthermore: "By what karma have I been born here, and to where must I go from this existence?"
How can he who possesses no discernment on this earth ever become inclined toward righteousness?
Therefore, it is appropriate that this desire to know "what is this? has arisen. What, then, is that triad of suffering?
To this he says: internal, [external, and superhuman].
The physical and the divine;
therein, the first is of two kinds.
It is both physical and mental.
Therein, physical suffering arises from the imbalance of the bodily constituents—wind, bile, and phlegm—and manifests as fever, dysentery, and so forth, pertaining to the self and the body.
Mental suffering is twofold, arising from separation from the beloved and union with the unpleasant.

This has been described as internal suffering (ādhyātmika-duḥkha). External suffering (ādhibhautika), however, is that which arises with reference to living beings (bhūta), caused by humans, domestic animals, birds, reptiles, and stationary beings. Supernatural suffering (ādhidaivika), moreover, is that which arises with reference to the divine (div), such as cold, heat, wind, rain, and so forth.
Thus, in one afflicted by these three kinds of suffering, a desire for knowledge arose in the brahmin of the Asuri clan.
In what domain?
In the cause that strikes down those [sufferings].
Regarding that cause which strikes down and destroys those three types of suffering,
he expresses the desire to know it:
"Are these sufferings [inherent] in the body?"
Or rather, is there some other person distinct from these [three] for whom these three sufferings arise; and furthermore, is there a means for their remedy or not?
If there is, then we shall rely upon that alone.
If we do not endure these [sorrows] like eunuchs with eyes closed at the onset of the first monsoon downpour,
then we are like one bitten by a scorpion who seeks a snake-charmer for an antidote, or one who cannot bear the pain arising from poison.
Thus, in that asura who was overwhelmed by unbearable suffering, a desire to know the cause for its destruction arose.
Seeking the absence of that arisen suffering, he took refuge in the Blessed One, the teacher Kapila, who is skilled in its remedy, thinking:
"He will explain the means for the remedy of the suffering I desire."
But surely, since the desire to know has arisen from sufferings themselves, how can it serve as the cause for their very non-existence?
For a son born from his own mother does not proceed to kill her.
True.
In this world, it is observed that whatever arises from something else may also become a cause of its own destruction.
For example, a crab or a mule, once born from its mother, brings about her very death.

Or, for instance, when a certain venomous serpent dwelling in a place thick with dry grass sees another snake approaching, it becomes enraged; the fire issuing from the breath of its mouth consumes the grass and even that serpent itself.
It has burned away [the doubt].
By this logic, the inquiry having arisen from sufferings themselves, it will bring about the very non-existence of those sufferings; such is the logical connection of the meaning.
To this, it is said: "If [the inquiry] were useless regarding what is already seen..."
The particle *ced* is used here in the sense of doubt;
the meaning is: "In this world, there is indeed a remedy for all the sufferings that have arisen, so what is the purpose of approaching Kapila?"
He demonstrates that very reason as it has been observed:

for all physical and internal diseases such as fever, dysentery, and so forth, there indeed exist physicians who are experts in the eight branches of Ayurveda, skilled in the treatment of the body, of foreign objects, of surgical probes, of poisons, of insanity, of impotence, of old age, and of childhood;
and for the internal torment of the mind, there is a remedy through union with pleasant things and by keeping unpleasant things at a distance.

The abandonment of the physical (ādhibhautika) [suffering] is possible through the conceptualization of villages, cities, and so forth; that of the celestial (ādhidaivika), by means of fanning, exposure to the sun, clothing, shelter, and the like. Therefore, the sense is: what is the use of approaching Kapila for the sake of those causes of affliction?
And thus there is a worldly proverb:
"If one should find honey on a sunbeam, why would he go to the mountain?
When the desired object is accomplished effortlessly, what wise man would resort to exertion?"
To this it is replied: No.
The word "no" here serves to negate the statement of the prima facie position;
the meaning is that it should not be stated in such a manner.
Because [remediation] is neither certain nor absolute;
that is, by the reasons you have stated, there is certainly no remedy.
For even when physicians apply potent medicines and strive to the best of their ability, a living being may at times—(p.3)—
Sometimes it fails and he lives;
even in a physician’s house, one sees the unavoidable death of wives, sons, spouses, brothers, fathers, and so forth—therefore, this is not an absolute remedy for internal suffering.
Furthermore, it is not a remedy even in the ultimate sense.
For even in the case of fevers and other ailments that have been rendered painless by medicine, it is observed that they arise again after a few days.
Therefore, in every respect, no remedy has been seen that is capable of providing an absolute removal of internal suffering,
just as the spring season and others, though they have passed away, return once more.
And there are verses on this point: "The burning sensation has arisen again; trembling has been born again;
hiccough afflicts him again; and fever has returned again."
And furthermore:
"A man with blossoming eyes, a probe-wielder, and a leper who practices internal medicine—these fools ask the physician: 'How is it that your children have died?'"
Moreover, there is no medicine through skill in the thorough knowledge of the elements; for it is said:
"Whatever roots one may grind with whatever [substance], and to whomever it should be given, it will become this or that."

Furthermore: Physicians, in order to consume the wealth of those seeking medical treatment and to demonstrate their own efficacy, intentionally aggravate even a minor ailment before them. Consequently, that very illness sometimes becomes incurable for them. And so it is said:
Physician, physician, homage to you who have destroyed all human suffering;
with the burden now placed upon you, this Kṛtānta prospers in happiness.
Thus, by means of this visible cause such as medicine and so forth, it is absolute—
necessarily,
ultimately, and in every respect.
There is no remedy for bodily suffering that is internal;
likewise, even through union with pleasant objects such as sounds, there is sometimes no cessation of mental suffering either.
Similarly, even suffering caused by external beings may sometimes be dispelled by means.
And sometimes it is not so;
likewise, even that which pertains to the divine (ādhidevika) sometimes departs and sometimes does not.
Furthermore, even the departure of suffering is purposeless because of its recurrence.
But for this disciple, the cause for the removal of suffering is intended to be both certain and ultimate;
therefore, it is appropriate to approach a teacher for that purpose.

If this is so, then let there be a cause consisting of sacrifices and the like—prescribed by the scriptures and taught in the *ānuśravika* [Veda]—which serves as a means to attain heaven and other such goals, even though it is distinct from what is perceived [in this world].
For even in the vault of heaven (*nākapṛṣṭha*), the threefold suffering is impossible;
and in that regard, a result that is either absolute (*ekāntika*) or final (*ātyantika*) is heard in the *ānuśrava*, the Veda.
The Veda is so called because disciples hear it subsequently from what has been spoken by the Guru;
that which exists therein is "ānuśravika.
This [means of knowledge], consisting of sacrifices and the like, is appropriate as a cause for the remedy of the threefold suffering.
For thus it is said: "He crosses over death,
he crosses over sorrow,
he crosses over evil."
“He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice overcomes even the murder of a Brāhmaṇa” (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 13.3.1.1).
And as for what the gods said to him once again— (p.4)
“We have drunk Soma; we have become immortal; we have reached the light; we have found the gods.
What can hostility now do to us? And what, O Immortal One, can the treachery of a mortal do?”
[Ṛgveda-saṃhitā 8.48.3] Thus it is said.
Here—in this scripture (śruti)—the fruit that is both certain and ultimate is heard.
Regarding this, the following is the explanation:
Once, it is said, Indra, having observed the gods assembled before him, spoke thus: "O gods, is there any happiness whatsoever other than that which comes from divinity?
Thereupon the gods replied: "There is no other happiness;
for this very reason, our dwelling is called *nāka* (the non-woeful)."
*Kam* is a name for happiness; its negation is *akam*, meaning unhappiness. Since that [unhappiness] does not exist there, it is called *nāka*.
It is nothing but pure happiness.
Two negatives convey the original meaning.
Thereupon Indra asked, "How so?
Then they replied, "For this reason, we have drunk—that is, we have consumed."
At the sacrifice, we have offered *soma*, the *soma* juice;
by drinking it, we have become immortal and have attained the state of gods. Furthermore, we have reached the light, that is, heaven.
Moreover: "We have not found [them]; we know the gods;
we know that in this heaven there are so many gods"—the word "what" (*kim*) is used here as an expression of censure.
"Nūnam" means certainly or for certain. "Asmān" is our [pronoun], with a change of case. "Kṛṇavat" means he shall do.
"Arāti" means the enemy, death.
Or rather, what will old age do to us,
we who are immortal mortals— mortals who drink the nectar of immortality?
The change in the wording is based on the rule: “*bahulaṃ chandasi*” [Pāṇini 2.4.73].
Likewise, for anyone else who shall drink the Soma, there will inevitably and certainly be an absolute and total destruction of the threefold suffering in every respect.
Therefore we say: what is the use of renunciation or the knowledge of Sāṅkhya? We shall perform that which is prescribed in the Vedas.
Having heard the statement of the Vedic proponents that heaven is a remedy for suffering, the Sāṅkhya teacher, in order to refute that and to establish his own system, spoke the second Āryā verse:
"The revealed [path] is like the perceptible; for it is impure, subject to decay, and characterized by excess.
Its opposite is superior, arising from the discernment of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower. (ISk 2)

That which has been described as the means for attaining heaven—namely, the Agnihotra and other rites based on traditional revelation (ānuśravika) and heard from scripture (śrauta)—is also, like the previously mentioned [empirical] remedies, an uncertain remedy against the threefold suffering.
For instance: "The wife desiring a son should eat the middle portion of the rice-ball," and "O ancestors, bestow a fetus" (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 2...).
33) Thus, with this mantra [Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 2.7.14], he eats many rice-balls—indeed more than a hundred—in accordance with the words of the Veda, until even a single son is born.
Likewise: "May we see a hundred autumns; may we live a hundred autumns" [Ṛgveda-saṃhitā 7.66].
Thus it stands in the Śruti.
However, [the sacrificer] dies while still in the womb, or as soon as born, or as a child, or even as a youth;
and furthermore, that scriptural cause is impure because its nature consists in the injury of animals.
Furthermore, that which is associated with decay [is subject] to downfall;
that which is associated with excellence [is also subject to it], because even there the relationship of master and servant is heard [in scripture]. And it has been said:
"Six hundred animals are sacrificed on the middle day."
"According to the statement regarding the horse sacrifice, it is deficient by three animals."

In the *Agniṣṭoma*, there is the slaughter of animals; in the *Gosava*, the slaughter of humans; in the *Sautrāmaṇī*, the drinking of *surā* liquor; and among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), there is unrestrained conversation with a widow. Furthermore, in the *Kalpasūtras*, many other forbidden acts are taught as things to be performed:
"One should sacrifice a Brāhmaṇa for Brahman, a Kṣatriya for the Kṣatra, a Vaiśya for the Maruts, a thief for Heat, and a killer of a hero for Hell" (*Taittirīya-brāhmaṇa* 3.4).
Because of such scriptural declarations as [Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 20.24.8],
and furthermore—
"Just as one cannot cleanse mud with mud, water with water, or liquor with liquor, even so one does not deserve to wipe away this killing of living beings with sacrifices."
[Bhāgavatapurāṇa 1.8.52]:
"For hands smeared with blood are not purified by blood alone.
[Śāṅkhāyanabrāhmaṇa 11]: "Just as men in this world eat animals, so do animals in the other world devour men; thus they experience the consequences."
Thus it is heard in the Veda. Furthermore: "If heaven is reached by cutting down trees, killing animals, and creating a mire of blood through sacrifices, then by what means is hell reached?"
Thus, that which is associated with impurity is in every respect a scriptural means for the remedy of the three types of suffering.
Now, as it was previously stated, "We have drunk Soma; we have become immortal," this is the response to that.
Even for those who drink the soma, such as Nṛga, Nahuṣa, Indra, and Yayāti, there were various kinds of afflictions resulting from bonds and imprisonment;
and for others, there was a fall [from heaven] due to the exhaustion of their karma.
Furthermore, it is observed that for rituals such as the *ekāha* sacrifices, which have a fixed number of days and thus a limited cause, the result—such as rebirth in heaven—is likewise limited.
Because the effect conforms to its cause,
a jar produced from a clay lump of a certain size must itself possess that same size.
Likewise, because the fruits of those actions based on traditional revelation (ānuśravika) have a finite measure, they are subject to exhaustion once again.
And it is characterized by intensity;
for example, as the poor man would suffer upon seeing the wealthy,
or the ugly man upon seeing the handsome.

Just as suffering arises for a fool upon seeing a wise man, or for one who possesses five celestial nymphs upon seeing a heavenly being with a hundred nymphs, or for one who possesses one nymph upon seeing that same being—
so too does this person perceive.
Thus, because of mutual superiority [among the gods], suffering is not absent even in heaven;
therefore,
that which is the opposite of this is better.

That cause which is the opposite and dissimilar to those two causes—the seen and the heard—which is certain, absolute, pure, inexhaustible, yielding infinite fruit, unsurpassed due to its isolation (kaivalya), and is therefore superior and praiseworthy—how does it come about? He says: "From the discernment of the Manifest, the Unmanifest, and the Knower."
The manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower—
through the discernment and experience of these three,
he becomes necessarily certain because of the granting of the fruit.

It is absolute due to knowledge of primordial nature (prakṛti); it is pure because of the possession of restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth; and it has inexhaustible fruit because there is no further re-entry [into bondage] upon the dissolution of the body.
The ellipsis of the sentence is that it is the unsurpassed fruit because of its isolation (*kaivalya*) and its state of being supreme.

In that context, the manifest (*vyakta*) consists of twenty-three categories due to the divisions of intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the sense organs (*indriya*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the gross elements (*bhūta*).
The unmanifest (*avyakta*) is primordial matter (*pradhāna*).
It is the cause of the manifestation of the manifest.
For there is no effect that is without a cause; thus is its establishment.
The Puruṣa is conscious.
By its mere presence, it is the cause of activity, like a magnet for iron;
therefore, it is established that this [Puruṣa] exists as the cause of the activity of the insentient Pradhāna.
These are the twenty-five principles (tattvas), known by the names Manifest (vyakta), Unmanifest (avyakta), and Knower (jña).
From the knowledge of which one is necessarily and in every way liberated from the threefold suffering.
Now, as to the question "In how many ways is there a division of these?", it is said here: "In four ways.
If it is asked "How so?", that is explained:
"Root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and modification."
The group of sixteen, however, is a transformation; the Puruṣa is neither a primary nature nor a transformation.
The root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is the primary matter (pradhāna) because it is the fundamental basis.
"Root" means the beginning of the seven natures and transformations;
it is called "nature" (prakṛti) by virtue of its function as the source.
Because it possesses the nature of production, it is the primal nature (*prakṛti*).
It is not a transformation (*vikṛti*), for it is not a transformation because it does not arise from anything else;
the meaning is that it is solely the cause, not the effect.

Because it is unproduced and because it produces [others], [Prakṛti] is neither an effect nor a cause. However, the seven beginning with Mahat—namely, Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, and the five tanmātras—are both causes and effects; these seven are causes insofar as they are the causes of other things.
And since the evolutes (*vikṛti*) themselves are effects, he states their manifestation therein: "From *pradhāna* comes *buddhi*"—thus it is an evolute;
and since that [intellect] produces the *ahaṅkāra*, it is a cause (*prakṛti*).

Ego (ahaṅkāra) is a modification because it is produced from the Great Principle (mahat); it is a primal nature (prakṛti) because it generates the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi). All five subtle elements are modifications because they are produced from ego.
From that, the five great elements (pañcamahābhūtāni) are born; thus they are the primary natures (prakṛti).
Because they have arisen and because they give rise [to others], the seven [principles] are both primary natures and transformations (vikṛti).
These are the subtle elements (tanmātra), known as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
The group of sixteen, moreover, is indeed a transformation (vikāra) because it is an effect;
however, it does not possess the nature of a primary cause (prakṛti) because it is not a cause.
He states its manifestation: the eleven organs are produced from the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) as a transformation, and the five gross elements are produced from the subtle elements (tanmātra).
This group of sixteen is a modification (*vikāra*); it has arisen from something else, but nothing else arises from it—this is the meaning.
This is because they have already arisen and because they do not produce [anything further].
The *puruṣa*, however, is neither primordial nature (*prakṛti*) because he does not produce [anything], nor is he a modification (*vikṛti*) because he has not arisen [from anything].
The meaning is that this is neither a cause nor an effect;
thus, it is both the primal nature (*prakṛti*) and the modification of the primal nature (*prakṛtivikṛti*).
Modification,
neither primary cause nor modification, and that which is neither— thus, through these four categories, the distinction between primary causes and modifications has been explained.

He states the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of establishing these objects of knowledge (*prameya*), namely the manifest (*vyakta*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the knower (*jña*).
For it is observed that the establishment of everything occurs through the sequence of the means of valid cognition, the objects of knowledge, the knower, and the act of knowing.
Perception (*dṛṣṭa*), inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative testimony (*āptavacana*) [are the means], because they are established as all the means of valid cognition.
Threefold is the means of valid cognition accepted, for the establishment of the objects of cognition proceeds from the means of valid cognition.
"Seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) is a synonym for direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That knowledge which arises in dependence upon the sense faculty (*akṣa*) is called direct perception or "seen.
For example, the five objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth, are the "seen" means of valid cognition for the [five] sense faculties, such as the ear and so forth.
This is the primary [function] of all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
When an object cannot be established by this [perception] when it is observed, there is scope for inference (anumāna);
and that [inference] possesses either three or five members of proof.
Others say that [inference] consists of three members or five members.
And that inference—which is free from the thirty-three fallacies—is extended when perception is absent.
It is called *anumāna* because, having observed some reason (*hetu*), one measures (*mīyate*) the object subsequent to that reason.
Just as, having observed smoke as the cause, the existence of fire is established—just as it was previously seen in a kitchen—this is inference (*anumāna*).

That object which cannot be established by means of perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference is [established] by the word of a reliable authority (*āptavacana*). For example: "There are apsarases in heaven."
The Nandana grove;
therein are the specific objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth;
and there is dwelling in celestial palaces (vimāna).
The authoritative persons (*āpta*) are those free from passion, hatred, and other defects, such as Brahmā and Sanatkumāra;
the scripture (*śruti*) is the Veda. That which is taught by these two is to be accepted as true; this is authoritative speech (*āptavacana*).

Now, one might object: "Are there not many other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as presumption (arthāpatti), probability (sambhava), non-existence (abhāva), intuition (pratibhā), tradition (aitihya), and analogy (upamāna)? How then can it be said that there are only three kinds of valid cognition?
To this it is replied: because they are all established by [these] three means of valid cognition. For indeed, all means of valid cognition are not in contradiction with these three.

In that regard, when it is said, "The fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," the meaning is that he eats at night; this presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) is nothing other than inference (*anumāna*). When "one *prastha*" is mentioned, the understanding that there are four *kuḍavas* is "possibility" (*sambhava*).
That too is indeed inference.
And non-existence (*abhāva*) is fourfold, distinguished as prior non-existence, mutual non-existence, non-existence through destruction, and absolute non-existence.
For example, by observing the drying of rice in the field, one establishes the non-existence of rain, thinking, "It has not rained."
That too is a variety of inference.
An example of intuitive cognition (*pratibhā*) is as follows:
"To the south of the Vindhya mountains and to the north of the Sahya mountains..."
On the earth, as far as the ocean, that region is most enchanting.
When this is said, the intuition arises that "there are excellent qualities" therein;
intuition is the knowledge of those who possess knowledge,
and that too is indeed inference.
Tradition (*aitihya*) is, for example, when people say, "A yakṣiṇī dwells in this banyan tree," and upon hearing this,
one gains the knowledge that she creates obstacles or bestows wealth and so forth.
That too is indeed inference.
As for analogy— such as "as is a cow, so is a gavaya"— that too is indeed inference.
Furthermore, [the inference is] from the cupped hands of one who is thirsty,
from the five fingers of one who is hungry,
and from the sight of large eyes and so forth in one who is weak.
Is it from the perception of mud on the pointing finger?
It is simply an inference, such as "there is knowledge," and so forth.
Therefore, it is correctly stated that the threefold means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established, since everything else is included within these three.

"Desired" (*iṣṭam*) means "intended" (*abhipretam*). He asks: what is to be established by that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? He says: "The establishment of the object of cognition (*prameya-siddhi*), for [it comes] from the means of valid cognition.
Because every object of cognition is measured by a means of valid cognition, just as sandalwood and the like are weighed by a scale.
It is like [measuring] ghee and the like by the *karṣa* and so forth, or rice and the like by the *prastha* and so forth;
direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*āgama*) are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are the manifest (*vyakta*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the knower (*jña*).
The knower (*pramātṛ*) is the Self (*ātman*). Among these, the manifest consists of twenty-three principles.
The unmanifest is the Pradhāna;
the knower is the Kṣetrajña.
Among these, some is cognized through direct perception, another through inference, and the remaining one through both authoritative testimony and inference.
Therefore, it was rightly stated by the Blessed Teacher: "For the establishment of the objects of cognition proceeds from the means of valid cognition."

Therein, the individual definitions of the three types of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are set forth: "Perception is the determinate cognition of each respective object; inference is declared to be of three kinds, preceded by the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin); and authoritative verbal testimony is the word of a reliable person. (ISk 5)

The determinative engagement of each of the five sense organs, such as the eye, with respect to each of their respective objects, such as form and so forth— that is perception (*pratyakṣa*), which consists of direct apprehension and is termed "the seen" (*dṛṣṭa*).
Inference (*anumāna*) is of three kinds.
Others say that the threefold proof consists of three members or five members;
that has been explained and stated.
The three-membered [proof] consists of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The thesis (*pakṣa*) is the statement of the proposition;
for example: "This place possesses fire.
The thesis is the presentation of the object to be proven.

The other fallacious positions (*pakṣābhāsa*) are the nine beginning with those contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣaviruddha*). The reason (*hetu*) possesses three characteristics (*trirūpa*). Furthermore, these three characteristics are: presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), existence in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattva*), and non-existence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣe asattva*).
An example of this is: "because of possessing smoke.
There are fourteen other fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), such as the unestablished (asiddha), the inconclusive (anaikāntika), the contradictory (viruddha), and so forth.
The illustration is of two kinds, by way of similarity and dissimilarity; for example, "the kitchen. There are ten other fallacious illustrations.
Thus, inference is devoid of the thirty-three appearances and consists of three members;
others say it consists of five members.

Regarding this, he says: "The members, moreover, are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the application (*upadeśana*), the illustration (*nidarśana*), the connection (*anusandhāna*), and the conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*)."

Thus, the demonstration of an object ascertained by oneself through a five-membered statement is the demonstration for the sake of others (*parārthapratipādana*), which is inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
And that is of three kinds:
*pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*.
In that case, one infers that rain will occur upon seeing the rising of exceptional clouds;
this is "as before" because it has been observed previously.
Or, there is the cognition that "it has rained above" upon seeing the swelling of a river.
The *śeṣavat* [inference] is as follows: having tasted a single drop of ocean water, the salty nature of the remainder is inferred; thus it is called *śeṣavat*.
The *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference] is as follows: [the inference of rain] from seeing a mango tree in flower.
Otherwise, it would be like saying, "The mango trees are in bloom," or again, for example, when one person says, "There is light outside," and another person also says the same.
The logical connection is that "the moon will rise.
Regarding the phrase "that is preceded by the mark and the bearer of the mark":

even though the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) is not perceived, he is established through the mark (*liṅga*), such as the sight of the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) and so forth, [in the form]: "Surely this person is a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) who possesses this triple staff."
But authoritative scripture (*āpta-śruti*) is the word of an authority (*āpta-vacana*);
it is the third means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Authorities (*āpta*) are teachers such as Brahmā and others.

*Śruti* means the Veda; thus, both of these constitute the word of an authoritative person (*āptavacana*). *Āpti* (attainment) is the direct realization of an object, which is the apprehension of things as they truly are. One who acts by means of that is an *āpta*—one who has directly perceived the *dharma* and grasps the meaning of what is heard through the attainment of reality. That which is spoken by such a person is called the word of an authoritative person. Furthermore, in that regard, there are three modes of verbal function (*śabdavṛtti*) due to the connection with well-known characteristics and qualities.

In this regard, there are three types of indication (*lakṣaṇā*): *jahallakṣaṇā*, *ajahallakṣaṇā*, and *jahadajahallakṣaṇā*. An extensive elaboration of these and others exists in the treatises on epistemology (*pramāṇa*).
Among those, we shall first set forth the doctrine of the Blessed One Kapila as it has been introduced.
For scripture is the word of a reliable person; the wise know a reliable person to be one whose defects have been eliminated.
One whose defects are exhausted could not utter a false statement, because the cause for doing so no longer exists.
One who is devoted to his own duty, free from attachment and aversion,
and is always honored by those of similar character— such a person should be known as a trustworthy authority.
Thus, this means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is of three kinds.

Thus, among the three types of means of valid cognition—perception and the rest—which establishes which of the categories known as the manifest (vyakta), the unmanifest (avyakta), and the knower (jña)? To this it is replied: "The cognition of supersensuous things arises from inference based on what is generally observed; that which remains unestablished even by that [inference] must be proven through the authoritative testimony of a reliable person. (ISk 6)
In this context, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and the *puruṣa* (spirit) are beyond the senses; their establishment occurs through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

For, having observed that the *liṅga* (the manifest world), beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), possesses the three qualities (*triguṇa*) and is an effect, it is established that there must exist an unperceived cause which is likewise characterized by the three qualities—this is what constitutes the *pradhāna*.
For it is impossible for existence to arise from non-existence.
Nor can the effect be dissimilar to its cause;
moreover, since the manifest world has already been established by direct perception itself, no further effort is required for that purpose.

Since even the insentient *pradhāna* engages in the act of production, there must necessarily exist a conscious *puruṣa*, like a magnet which is the cause of the power for the iron to move; thus is the existence of the Knower proven.
Is it not the case that the view— that whatever object is not perceived by direct perception does not exist in any way whatsoever— is consistent?
For example, a second head of a non-divine being,
or a third arm.
Or like a hare’s horn and so forth.
To dispel the doubt that "in this way, since the *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa* are not perceived, they too do not exist," he says:
"Because of excessive distance, because of proximity, because of injury to the sense organs, and because of the instability of the mind..."
Due to subtlety, obstruction, overpowering, and intermixture with similar things. // ISk_7 //
In this world, there are eight ways in which even existing things are not perceived.

To demonstrate this: for example, although Devadatta, Viṣṇumitra, and Yajñadatta exist, they are not perceived because they have gone to another country and are too far away. Does it follow, then, that they do not exist?
Or, just as the eye does not perceive collyrium due to extreme proximity,
does that mean it does not exist?
Or, just as the deaf and the blind do not perceive sound and form [respectively]?
So, do they not exist? With their minds unsettled, they do not even see the king as he passes by.
So, has he not gone?
The atoms of smoke, heat, dust, and mist are not perceived;
does this mean they do not exist?
[No,] for that which is obstructed by a wall is not perceived.
Is it then that they do not exist?
Since planets, lunar mansions, stars, and so forth are not perceived when overwhelmed by the light of the sun and other luminaries, can one imagine their non-existence?
Or, if something thrown into a heap of mud, a cluster of blue lotuses, myrobalan fruits, pearls, or pigeons is not perceived because it is identical [to the rest], does that mean it is non-existent?
Is it then that [the object] does not exist? Thus has the non-apprehension of even existing things been stated in eight ways; now, the non-apprehension of non-existent things occurs in four ways.

To this it is replied: [the distinction is] due to the difference between antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
Among these, antecedent non-existence is as follows: the jar is not perceived in the lump of clay prior to its production.
Destruction is, for example, when the jar, having been destroyed by the blow of a hammer, is no longer perceived.
Mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is, for example, the absence of "cowness" in a horse, or the absence of "horseness" in a cow.
Absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is, for example, a second head on the Lord (*anīśvara*).
The third [type] is a non-existent arm, or things such as a rabbit's horn;
thus, this non-apprehension is twelvefold.
For the wise perceive it in eight ways, while the unwise perceive it in four;
likewise, although both Pradhāna and Puruṣa exist, they are not perceived [as such].
Among these [categories], by what cause are these two not perceived? It is said:
their non-perception is due to subtlety, not due to non-existence; their perception occurs through their effects.
And that effect, beginning with the Great One (mahat), is both dissimilar and similar to its primal source (prakṛti).
The non-perception and non-comprehension of that *pradhāna* is due to its subtlety (*saukṣmya*), not because of its non-existence.
The *pradhāna* is subtle because it lacks the characteristics of sound and so forth, like atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like;
however, it is not [non-existent] in this way.
If it were non-existent, then the primal matter (pradhāna) would not be perceived;
however, the primal matter does exist but is not perceived due to its subtlety, like atoms and so forth.
If that is so, how then is it perceived?
To this, he says: its apprehension is through its effect (*kāryataḥ*).
Having observed the effect, the cause is to be inferred, like a *vaṭadhānya* seed.
Just as the cause, the *vaṭadhānya* seed, is inferred upon observing the effect, the *vaṭa* tree.
Thus, the existent *pradhāna* alone is inferred as the cause of the existent effects, such as the *mahat* and so forth;
for indeed, the production of the existent from the non-existent does not occur.
The group beginning with the *mahat* consists of twenty-three members: the *mahat*, the *ahaṅkāra*, the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*), the eleven organs, and the five gross elements.

Observing this effect, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), which consists of the three qualities (triguṇa), it is inferred that there exists a Pradhāna as its cause, which likewise consists of the three qualities, of which this three-qualitative effect is the result. Furthermore, that effect is both dissimilar and similar to its material cause (prakṛti).
The meaning is that [the effect] is both dissimilar and similar to the *pradhāna*.
There exist those causes by which this *pradhāna* is both dissimilar and similar [to its effects].
For example, in the world, a son may be similar or dissimilar to his father; if he is similar in form, then he is not so in qualities.
The meaning is that when [he was recognized] by his qualities, he was not [recognized] by his physical form;
and we shall explain those reasons further below.
Let this matter rest for now;
let us ask something else: does this [evolute] beginning with the Mahat arise while already existing within the Pradhāna prior to its production, or does it come into being as something non-existent?

In this regard, there is a disagreement among the teachers, and therefore a doubt arises. On this point, the Vaiśeṣikas disagree; they maintain that "the existent comes from the non-existent," for they are convinced that the jar does not exist in the lump of clay prior to its production.
"Wretched living beings [speculate] 'it exists' or 'it does not exist';
neither exists nor does not exist—
this is the position of the Buddhists."
Thus, among these philosophical systems that propound mutually contradictory views, what indeed can be the certainty?
To this it is said:
first of all, the Jīvakas, who maintain the doctrine of both existence and non-existence, are refuted by the very contradiction within their own words.
If it exists, then it is not non-existent; nor, if it is non-existent, can there be existence.
This is because existence and non-existence are contradictory in a single locus.
In this regard, the analogy is like saying "Devadatta, who is dead, lives.
However, for the Buddhists, because they do not adopt a position of either "it exists" or "it does not exist," it is not even appropriate to engage in discussion with them.
But for the Vaiśeṣikas, who hold the view that "what was non-existent becomes existent," the following is stated in order to refute that doctrine:
Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, because there is the grasping of a material cause, because everything is not possible from everything,
because the efficient cause produces only that for which it has the capacity, and because of the nature of the cause, the effect exists [in the cause].
In this world, only that which exists truly comes into being; there is no production of what does not exist.
If it were otherwise, then oil would arise from sand.
A cloak made from the hair of a tortoise,
the playful arching of the eyebrows of a barren woman's daughter,
and the horn of a hare.
And [if it were otherwise], it would be like a flower in the sky;

yet it does not exist [in that way]. Therefore, it is inferred that prior to its production, the Great One (mahat) and the other evolutes certainly exist within the Primal Matter (pradhāna), because of the grasping of the material cause (upādāna).
In this world, whoever desires something takes hold of its means of acquisition; they grasp that which is the cause for it. For example, one who desires curd takes hold of milk.
Furthermore, if the effect were non-existent [in the cause], then one seeking curd would also take up water;
yet one does not do so.
Therefore, the effects such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest exist within the Pradhāna.
Furthermore, because there is no arising of everything from everything:
in this world, whatever exists within something arises from that very thing;
as, for example, oil from sesame seeds.
Clarified butter comes from curd.

If the effect were pre-existent [in the cause], then everything would arise from everything; consequently, silver, gold, jewels, pearls, coral, and so forth would be produced from grass, dust, sand, and the like.
And yet they do not arise;

therefore, we see that because everything cannot possibly arise from everything, the effects such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest must already exist in the Pradhāna before they come into being.
For this reason, it exists: "because the capable [cause] produces what is possible."

In this world, a capable artisan, endowed with the necessary instruments, materials, time, and means, undertakes only a task that is possible from what is possible, and not an impossible task from what is impossible. For example, a capable potter, equipped with a workable lump of clay and provided with a staff, wheel, string, water, and a lathe, is seen to produce jars, bowls, and water-jars,
but not large storage jars (*maṇika*) and the like.
Because it is impossible for that [effect] to exist within such a mass;
for if there were no restriction regarding the instrument, one might attempt to produce even the impossible from the impossible.
Therefore, the effect must exist [in the cause], not be non-existent.
Furthermore: because of the existence of the cause, the effect must also exist as a reality.
In this world, whatever the characteristics of the cause are, such will be the characteristics of the effect.
Just as *kodrava* grains arise from *kodrava* seeds and rice arises from rice seeds,
if the effect were non-existent [prior to its production], then rice would also be produced from *kodrava* seeds.
And yet it does not exist [as a separate entity].
Therefore, from the existence of the cause as well, we see that the effects such as the Great One (mahat) and the rest exist within the Pradhāna.
Thus, by these five reasons, it has been established that the effect exists [in the cause].

"Verily, my dear, in the beginning this was Being alone, one only without a second; regarding this, some say that in the beginning this was Non-being alone," starting thus, the Śruti continues until: "Verily, my dear, in the beginning this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
In this regard, concerning what was stated in the preceding verse— that [the manifest] is both dissimilar and similar to its nature (prakṛti)—
this [verse] is commenced in order to demonstrate their similarity and dissimilarity:
"It is caused, impermanent, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, and indicative."
The manifest is composed of parts and is dependent; the unmanifest is the opposite.
"Having a cause" (*hetumat*): that which has a cause of its arising is "having a cause.
Cause (*hetu*), designation (*apadeśa*), motive (*nimitta*), primal matter (*prakṛti*), and causal factor (*kāraṇa*) are synonymous.
These are synonyms for the Pradhāna.

Therefore, by reason of the Pradhāna, this twenty-three-fold subtle body (liṅga), beginning with Mahat and ending with the gross elements, possesses a cause. For instance: Mahat, which is the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), has the Pradhāna as its cause.
Therefore, it is said that from this [ego] arise the eleven organs and the subtle elements (tanmātras), and from those, the gross elements;
thus, all of this is mutually caused.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of causes: the productive (kāraka) and the informative (jñāpaka).
In this regard, the fourfold causal agent consists of *pradhāna*, intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
The fourfold informing agent consists of five types based on the distinctions of error (*viparyaya*), incapacity (*aśakti*), contentment (*tuṣṭi*), and attainment (*siddhi*).
Thus, it is established that this [world] possesses causes, being endowed with these two kinds of causes.
Furthermore: it goes to destruction because it is impermanent;
since it possesses origination, it is therefore impermanent.
That which is devoid of a cause is permanent—this is the definition of the permanent.
This [universe] is the opposite of that; therefore, it is impermanent.
For example: a jar produced from a lump of clay is observed to be impermanent;
likewise, the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest are produced from Pradhāna.

Therefore, it is impermanent and dissolves back into that very [source]. To explain: at the time of dissolution, the intellect (*buddhi*) dissolves into primordial matter (*pradhāna*); the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) dissolves into that [intellect]; the sense organs and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) dissolve into that [ego]; and the gross elements (*bhūta*) dissolve into those [subtle elements]. Therefore, it is impermanent.
Furthermore— “non-pervasive” means not omnipresent;
the meaning is that this [space] is not like *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*, which are omnipresent,
for this exists only in the very location where it is situated.
Furthermore, it is active;
because at the time of transmigration, the effects such as the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth transmigrate by depending upon the subtle body, it is therefore active.
Furthermore, it is manifold, being of many kinds, consisting of twenty-three types.
And the other is the dependent (*āśrita*). Whatever arises from something is dependent upon that;
cognition (*buddhi*) is dependent upon primordial matter (*pradhāna*).
And egoity depends upon that [intellect], as do the sense organs, the subtle elements, and those gross elements.
Thus it is supported;
it is called a *liṅga* because it undergoes dissolution (*laya*);
that is, it possesses parts.
They are called "parts" (*avayava*) because they go toward [the whole], just as the hands, feet, and so forth belong to a body.
A manifest entity (*vyakta*) is endowed with parts such as sound, touch, taste, form, and smell.
Furthermore, it is "dependent" (*paratantra*), meaning it is reliant upon another.
Just as a son is not independent while his father is alive, so it is with the manifest;
the intellect (buddhi) is dependent on primordial matter (pradhāna), and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is dependent on the intellect.
The sense faculties and the subtle elements are dependent on the ego;
the gross elements are dependent on the subtle elements.
Thus it is "dependent on another."
The manifest has been described;
the unmanifest possesses characteristics opposite to these:
it is without cause because it is unproduced.
It is eternal because it lacks a cause;
it is all-pervasive because it is omnipresent.
Pervading everything from Brahma down to a blade of grass like a person, the Pradhāna remains established.
It is inactive because it sows all things;
it is one because it is the cause of all;
it is independent because it is sovereign.
It is without marks because it is unproduced;
it is partless because it is formless;
it is independent because it is the cause of the arising of all things.

Thus, by this noble [verse], the dissimilarity between the Manifest and the Unmanifest has been stated. Their similarity is now being described: "It consists of the three qualities, is non-discriminative, is an object, is common, is insentient, and has the nature of productivity."
The Manifested is thus, as is the Primal Nature; and the Spirit is the opposite of both.
The manifest, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), consists of the three qualities;
the Pradhāna also consists of the three qualities,
because the effect conforms to its cause.
Just as when black threads are the cause, the cloth which is the effect is also necessarily black;
since the effect possesses the three qualities (triguṇa), its cause must also possess the three qualities—thus the Pradhāna is established.
Furthermore: the manifest is non-discriminative (aviveki).
It is not possible to distinguish them by saying, "these are the qualities" and "this is the manifest";
likewise, it is impossible to separate the Pradhāna by saying, "this is the Pradhāna" and "these are the qualities.
Furthermore, the object is the manifest, beginning with the Mahat.
That [Prakṛti] is the object of enjoyment for the Puruṣa by virtue of its nature as pleasure, pain, and delusion;
for he is its enjoyer.
Likewise, Pradhāna is also the object of enjoyment for all Puruṣas, who are the knowers of the field (kṣetrajña).
The universal is manifest,
like a courtesan [who belongs] to all men;
so too is primordial matter (*pradhāna*).
The manifest is insentient;
it does not perceive pleasure, pain, or delusion,
and the same applies to the primal matter (pradhāna).
The manifest possesses the nature of procreation:
from the intellect (buddhi) arises the ego (ahaṅkāra), from that the sense organs and the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi), and from those the gross elements (bhūtāni) are born;
in this same way, the primary cause (pradhāna) also produces the intellect.
This similarity between the manifest and the unmanifest has been stated.
Now, that which was stated as "the person (puruṣa) is the reverse of that and likewise," is being demonstrated.

He is the opposite of those two, the manifest and the unmanifest. Whatever common properties they possess—namely, that which was stated as "consisting of the three guṇas, non-discriminative, objective, general, insentient, and productive"—he is the opposite of that; he possesses different characteristics.
It is devoid of qualities, discriminative, beyond the scope of the senses, unique, conscious, and devoid of the property of productivity.

Having stated the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), he states the similarity (*sādharmya*) with the words: "And likewise the Spirit (*puruṣa*). [The verse continues: "The manifest (*vyakta*) is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, indicative, composed of parts, and subordinate; the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the opposite."
Thus it has been said in the *Sāṅkhyakārikā* (verse 10):
"Just as the Pradhāna is dissimilar to the Manifested, so too is the Puruṣa similar in nature to the Pradhāna.
For he is without cause, eternal, all-pervading, inactive, one, independent, without marks, partless, and sovereign. (SkMv_11)

In this regard, it has been stated that the manifest (vyakta) consists of the three qualities (triguṇa), while the unmanifest (avyakta) and the Puruṣa are devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). Of what nature are these qualities? To this it is replied: they consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion; their purposes are illumination, activity, and restraint.
And the qualities (guṇas) function through mutual suppression, subsistence, production, and companionship.
In this regard, the summary is as follows:

those qualities whose nature (*ātman*)—that is, their own essence (*svarūpa*)—consists of pleasure (*prīti*), displeasure (*aprīti*), and dejection (*viṣāda*), are said to be "having pleasure, displeasure, and dejection as their nature.
Their defining characteristics are now stated.
In this context, *sattva* consists of joy (*prīti*). The word "self" (*ātman*) refers to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Why? Because its characteristic is pleasure (*sukha*).

For whatever person obtains joy anywhere, one should understand that their *sattva* consists of straightforwardness, gentleness, truthfulness, purity, modesty, intelligence, forbearance, compassion, knowledge, and so forth;
whereas *rajas* is characterized by lack of joy.
Why? Because its defining characteristic is suffering.

For whenever anyone experiences displeasure anywhere, there—along with hatred, malice, envy, censure, arrogance, longing, deceit, fraud, binding, killing, and mutilation—that should be understood as *rajas*; and that which consists of despondency is *tamas*.
Why? Because its characteristic is delusion (*moha*).

For whenever anyone perceives delusion (*moha*) anywhere, therein one should recognize *tamas* as ignorance, intoxication, laziness, fear, dejection, unfitness for action, atheism, despondency, sleep, and so forth.
Furthermore: [the qualities] have illumination, activity, and restraint as their purposes.
"Those whose objects are illumination, activity, and restraint" means those [guṇas] for whom these are their respective purposes.
Among them, "it must be illuminated" refers to sattva;
"it must be set in motion" refers to rajas.

"It is to be restrained" and "it is to be withdrawn" refers to *tamas*. Furthermore: "The *guṇas* function through mutual suppression, support, production, and companionship. In this regard, there is also a summary verse: The *guṇas* have the nature of mutually suppressing, supporting, producing, and being companions to one another. Among these, the summary is as follows: When one *guṇa* predominates, it suppresses the others; it supports them by providing a basis for their manifestation; it produces effects in conjunction with them; and they exist as companions, never acting alone. Thus, the three *guṇas*—*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—are always in a state of mutual interaction.
Those qualities for which there exist mutual overcoming, mutual support, mutual production, mutual companionship, and mutual functions are described as such.
The word "ca" (and) should be understood as indicating a conjunction.
Furthermore, joy and the other [qualities] have already been mentioned previously.

And there is mutual suppression: through the suppression of *rajas* and *tamas*, a tranquil modification (*vṛtti*) of *sattva* arises, such as virtue (*dharma*) and so forth; through the suppression of *sattva* and *tamas*, a terrible modification of *rajas* arises, such as non-virtue (*adharma*) and so forth;
through the suppression of *sattva* and *rajas*, a deluded modification of *tamas* arises, such as ignorance (*ajñāna*) and so forth.
Furthermore: the qualities (guṇas) are mutually dependent.
For sattva, depending upon activity and restraint, brings about illumination; rajas, depending upon illumination and restraint, brings about activity.
It regulates [the qualities] by resorting to their activities of darkness and light;
these are to be understood as being like the support of a triple staff.
Furthermore: "The qualities give birth to one another."
They produce one another:
sometimes *sattva* produces *rajas* and *tamas*; sometimes *tamas* produces *sattva* and *rajas*.
Just as a lump of clay, presided over by a potter together with his equipment, produces a jar, so too do they produce [their effects].
It is accepted that they mutually awaken one another,
just as Devadatta and Yajñadatta awaken each other.
Thus, the qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—residing in the intellect (buddhi) mutually awaken one another.
In this way, the qualities are mutual producers.
Furthermore, the qualities are mutual companions.
Because they possess the nature of being inseparable;
for thus it is said:
"Rajas has sattva as its mate, and sattva has rajas as its mate."
The union of both *sattva* and *rajas* is called *tamas*.
Furthermore, another point: the *guṇas* function reciprocally; they produce the functioning of one another. (Devībhāgavatapurāṇa 3.50)
Just as a certain woman, endowed with charm, modesty, grace, and playful elegance, generates affection for her husband and her own circle of kinsmen,
yet that very same woman generates suffering and delusion among her co-wives;
even so, by means of the quality of *sattva* acting as a woman, the activity of *rajas* and *tamas* is produced.
In this same way, it should be applied to the others as well.
Here it is said: Sattva, rajas, and tamas are certainly not of different natures.
Why?
Because they abide within their own inherent natures.
In this world, indeed, a woman endowed with beauty, youth, courtesy, great goodness, mindfulness, intense emotion, and the playful grace of amorous gestures is taught to be the very form of *sattva*.
She brings happiness to her husband,
but causes suffering to her co-wives and delusion to those possessed by passion.
Likewise, when the kṣatriyas strike down an army of bandits that has committed offenses by inflicting suffering, this is taught as being the form of *rajas*.
And through that, it brings happiness to those who were harassed and oppressed by the bandits,
while causing pain and delusion to the bandits themselves.

Likewise, a dense, dark black cloud— swollen with water, hanging low, as if swallowing the sky and the earth, increasing in size, accompanied by cranes, lightning, and deep thunder— is designated as "the form of darkness.
And that [cloud] is a source of joy for farmers who have prepared their seeds and implements.

It alone is the cause of suffering and delusion for women whose husbands are away from home—those who have not provided shelter, who have not prepared portions of food, oil, and salt, and who have not trimmed the grass and wood.
Thus, because its nature is established in this way, there is only one [principle], namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
To this it is replied: these three are distinct classes of entities.
Because their characteristics are established as distinct.
If it is asked how so, it is said:
Sattva is held to be light and illuminating; rajas is stimulating and mobile.
The very covering of the Guru is darkness; its function is like that of a lamp, by way of its purpose.
In this regard, that which was stated in the preceding Āryā verse is the characteristic of *sattva*, as well as the characteristic that manifests lightness.
When *sattva* is predominant in Devadatta, then his limbs are light,
and his sense faculties become pure and capable of grasping their respective objects.
Then it should be understood that today my *sattva* exists in a state of intensity;
and because it is the cause for accomplishing one's desired nature, it is so.
*Rajas*, on the other hand, is stimulating and mobile.
"Supporting" means that which impels, namely the upward channel (*unnāḍi*);
just as an intoxicated bull becomes exultant upon seeing another bull, so too [is this].
Alternatively, the meaning is that pride is a flickering activity.
Thus, in whichever person—whether Devadatta or Yajñadatta—the quality of passion (*rajas*) becomes predominant, he seeks out quarrels.
Furthermore, his mind becomes restless, thinking, "I shall go to the village," "I desire a woman," "I shall perform austerities," and so forth. In this way, his mind is constantly agitated.
This is the characteristic of *rajas*. Regarding *tamas*, it is said: *tamas* is indeed heaviness and obscuration;
that which possesses heaviness and the quality of veiling is *tamas*.
When the limbs become heavy and the sense faculties become sluggish, incapable of grasping their respective objects,
then one should consider that darkness prevails in its intensity.
Therefore, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are indeed distinct categories.
Furthermore, regarding what was further asserted— that a woman, a Kṣatriya, and a cloud—
concerning these three as well, we say this:
Sattva, depending upon rajas and tamas, enters into a relationship of mutual subservience (aṅgāṅgibhāva) by means of its own nature;
from its impairment, suffering arises.
In the same way, this should be applied to rajas and tamas.
To the question of how there can be a single operation (*vṛtti*) of qualities that are mutually contradictory, he says: "For enemies who are mutually contradictory do not accomplish a single purpose;
yet these qualities, although mutually contradictory, accomplish the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*)."
Why?
Because its functioning is according to its object, like a lamp; "like a lamp" means similar to a lamp.
In terms of purpose, that is, by virtue of the task at hand,
the functioning of even these mutually contradictory things is observed;
for example, through the conjunction of oil, fire, and a wick, even substances that are mutually contradictory combine to produce a single effect.
Just as they produce a form consisting of light, so too the qualities (guṇas), though mutually opposed, act together to accomplish the purpose of the Puruṣa.
Here it is asked: this is indeed an intermediate question.

Regarding what was stated in the preceding verse—that "the manifest is composed of the three *guṇas*, non-discriminative, objective, common, insentient, and productive"—how is it known that the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is likewise endowed with the possession of the three *guṇas* and so forth? To this, it is replied:

The properties of non-discrimination and so forth are established because [the manifest] consists of the three guṇas; because their opposites are absent [in the unmanifest], and because the effect has the nature of the qualities of its cause, the Unmanifest is also established.
This group beginning with non-discrimination and ending with the property of productivity, which is established in the manifest (vyakta), is also established in the unmanifest (avyakta).
How is this known?
From the fact of the three qualities (traiguṇya).
That which consists of the three guṇas is undiscriminated; that which is undiscriminated is an object;
that which is an object is common.

That which is general is insentient; that which is insentient has the nature of productivity. Therefore, the quality of non-discrimination and so forth is established precisely from the fact of the three gunas.
Because the opposite of that does not exist;
for here, wherever there are threads, right there is the cloth, and wherever there is the cloth, right there are the threads;
he who sees the threads sees the cloth.
Or, just as one who sees a cloth sees its threads,
even so is the relationship between the manifest and the unmanifest, like that between the cloth and the threads;
for the primary cause (pradhāna) is at a distance, while the manifest is close at hand.
For he who perceives the manifest also perceives the unmanifest;
or rather, the yogi who perceives the Pradhāna also perceives the manifest.
Therefore, because there is no absence of error, the unmanifest is established by the group of qualities beginning with non-discrimination.
It is established from this as well:
because the effect consists of the qualities of its cause, the unmanifest is also established.

"Qualities of the cause" (kāraṇaguṇāḥ) means the qualities belonging to the cause; that which has these as its essence—that is, its own nature—is "consisting of the qualities of the cause" (kāraṇaguṇātmakatvam).
The word "ātman" (self) refers to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
because an effect possesses the intrinsic nature of its causes. In this world, whatever the nature of the instrument may be, the effect likewise comes to possess that very same nature.
Because the effect conforms to its cause:
just as from a pungent nimba tree only a pungent juice arises, and from something sweet, a sweet juice such as that of grapes arises;
therefore, the unmanifest (avyakta) is established by the group of qualities beginning with non-discrimination (aviveki).

In this regard, as for what was stated by you—that it is known how the Unmanifest (avyakta) is endowed with the group of qualities beginning with non-discrimination (aviveka)—that has been established precisely in this way by means of three reasons.
Here [the opponent] says: "In this world, that which is not perceived does not exist."
Just as a second head of the non-creator (Ishvara),
a third hand,
or a hare's horn.
Or [like] the playful movements of the eyebrows of the son of a barren woman and so forth;
since the Pradhāna and Puruṣa are not perceived at all, how indeed can it be understood that they exist?
The quantity of the masses of stones on the Himalayas cannot be apprehended; does that mean it does not exist?
In the same way, although the primary cause (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa) are not directly perceived, they are nevertheless apprehended through logical reasons.
And we shall explain those reasons further below.
They are stated as follows:

"Because of the finite measure of distinct objects, because of their commonality, because of their activity proceeding from a power, because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-distinction of the manifold universe. (ISk 15)
Primal Matter (pradhāna) exists. Why? Because of the finite measure of differentiated effects.
In the world, wherever there is an agent, a finite measure is observed.

Just as a potter fashions from a limited lump of clay a limited jar that holds a *prastha* or an *āḍhaka*, so too is the manifest (*vyakta*) limited. It consists of twenty-three principles: one intellect (*buddhi*), one ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), eleven organs (*indriya*), and five gross elements (*mahābhūta*).
Having thus observed this manifest world to be finite, we establish by inference that there exists its cause, the Pradhāna, which produces this manifest world that is finite.
If the Pradhāna were not the cause, this manifest world would be infinite; yet it possesses finitude. Therefore, the Pradhāna exists.
For this reason as well, [the cause] exists, because we observe a commonality.
Of what is there this commonality?
Precisely of the individual effects.
For this very reason, there is a complete correspondence consisting merely of fragments and shards;
having seen ornaments and the like, he demonstrates them as they truly are.
From the general context, it is observed that among the various divisions of the world, there is a correspondence with each individual genus.
Their nature is one of conformity;
therefore, from the observation of this conformity, we see that the Pradhāna exists as the cause.
For this reason also it exists: because of the activity [of the world] proceeding from potentiality.
In this world, whatever is capable of a particular purpose operates only toward that purpose;
for example, a potter is capable of producing jars, small pots, bowls, water-filters, and so forth.
Therefore, we establish that the Pradhāna also possesses a capacity, by means of which capacity it produces the manifest (vyakta).
And that power cannot be without a substratum;
therefore, the Pradhāna exists, wherein the power resides. For this reason as well, it exists: because of the distinction between cause and effect.
It is called a cause (kāraṇa) because it acts; it is called an effect (kārya) because it is acted upon; [the term] "from their distinction" refers to those two.
For example, the lump of clay is the cause and the jar is the effect.
Indeed, it is the jar alone that is capable of holding honey, water, milk, and so forth, whereas the lump of clay is not.
Such is the distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest.

The manifest (vyakta) is other [than the unmanifest], consisting of everything from the Great Principle (mahat), ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra), the subtle elements (tanmātra), the sense organs, up to the gross elements (mahābhūta); and that is the effect (kārya).
Furthermore, the unmanifest (avyakta), the Primal Matter (pradhāna), is the opposite of that, being the cause (kāraṇa).
Therefore, the Pradhāna exists. For this reason as well, it exists: because of the non-differentiation of the manifold world. Non-differentiation means the absence of differentiation.
The state of having all forms is *vaiśvarūpya*;
the meaning is "multiform.
Of that.
The three worlds go to non-distinction within the five great elements;
the five great elements go to non-distinction within the subtle elements;
and the five subtle elements and the eleven organs go to non-distinction within the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra).
Egoity resides in the intellect,
and that [intellect] resides in the Pradhāna.
Thus, at the time of dissolution, the three worlds remain undifferentiated within the Pradhāna.
It is called *pradhāna* because everything is held (*dhīyate*) and established (*sthāpyate*) within it in its entirety;
for from that, during creation, only what exists (*sat*) manifests.
Indeed, there is no arising of the non-existent (*asat*), nor the destruction of the existent (*sat*).

“There is no being for the non-existent, nor is there non-being for the existent,” as stated in the *Bhagavadgītā* (2.16); and from the *Śruti*: “In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed Being alone” (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1).
For example: curd and other such products exist indeed, undifferentiated within the milk prior to their production.
If production were from the non-existent, then a jar or other objects would be produced even from a piece of wood;
yet this does not occur.

Therefore, it is correct that the production of a jar and other such things occurs from the cause— the lump of clay— as something already existing. Just as this manifold variety of tastes, smells, and so forth exists undifferentiated within water and earth [in relation] to stationary beings, and within stationary beings [in relation] to moving beings,
so too, through the non-interruption of the genus, everything has everything as its essence.
"There exists a Pradhāna, wherein the marks such as Mahat and the rest go to a state of non-distinction.
Thus, that Pradhāna is necessarily characterized by a subsequent manifestation of distinction following a period of non-distinction. To this, it is replied:
"The unmanifest cause exists; it proceeds from the three *guṇas* and from their combination."
By way of transformation, it is like water, due to the specific distinctions of the substrates for each respective quality.
"The unmanifest is the cause.
Thus, by these five reasons, it is known that there exists a single cause for this world, which is the unmanifest root.
Here [an objection] is raised: "If the *pradhāna* is one, how then does it produce manifold effects?"
For instance, a single thread does not produce the effect known as a cloth;
likewise, it is not tenable that the single Pradhāna produces multiple effects. Therefore, it is resolved: "It proceeds by way of the three qualities (guṇas)."

For multiplicity arises from the existence of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* within the *pradhāna*; therefore, worldly activity proceeds in three ways by virtue of the three qualities,
and also from their combination.

Just as the currents in the Ganges, when united, originate the Ganges, or as threads, when combined, produce a cloth, so too the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—when united while abiding in the Pradhāna, produce the manifest (vyakta).
Here it is said: In this world, there are two kinds of causes, because of their nature as transformers (pariṇāmaka).
And because of the absence of transformation.
In that regard, we perceive the lump of clay, the staff, the string, the water, and the potter's wheel as being non-transformative;
yet, through transformation, milk becomes curd.
In this regard, as to how the Pradhāna is the cause, it is said here: "through transformation.
Just as milk transforms into the state of curd—such that what is milk is itself the curd.
In this way, the primary cause (pradhāna) transforms into the state of the manifest (vyakta).
The meaning is that the manifest is like curd and the primary cause is like milk;
that which is unmanifest is itself the manifest.
Therefore it is said that primordial matter (pradhāna) is the cause by way of transformation.
To this, he asks: what is the illustration? It is said: like water.
Just as a single body of water transforms into the state of snow on the Himalayas,
and just as sugarcane juice transforms into the states of *rasikā*, *ṣaṇḍa*, *matsarikā*, sugar, molasses, and jaggery;
or just as milk transforms into the states of curd, whey, fresh butter, clarified butter, *ariṣṭa*, *kilāṭa*, *kūrcikā*, and so forth.
In this very way, the unmanifest transforms into the internal state consisting of intellect, ego, the subtle elements, the senses, and the gross elements;
it transforms into the celestial state consisting of cold, heat, wind, rain, and so forth.
Here one asks: since the three worlds have arisen from a single Pradhāna, how is it that they are so diverse?

In this world, those who are gods are happy, humans are suffering, and animals are deluded. Since the three worlds have arisen from a single primary cause (*pradhāna*), how is it that there is such disparity among them, characterized by delusion and so forth? To this it is replied: "Because of the specific differences in the substrata of each respective quality (*guṇa*).
For example: water falling from the sky has but a single taste.
And having reached the earth, that [substance] attains various flavors due to the differences among distinct vessels;
likewise, these three worlds, though produced from the single *pradhāna*, have attained a state of differentiation through the inequality of the *guṇas*.

Just as among the gods the quality of sattva is predominant, they are therefore happy; yet even there, rajas and tamas exist in a subordinate manner. Among humans, rajas is predominant, and therefore they are miserable.
In those [beings] as well, there exist both *sattva* and *tamas*. Among those born in the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*), *tamas* is predominant; therefore, they are deluded.
Even in them, however, *sattva* and *rajas* are present.
Thus, there arises a disparity among the three worlds produced from a single [source].
Thus, through these two noble verses, the realization of *pradhāna* has been accomplished.
Hereafter, we shall treat the realization of the *puruṣa*.
To this, an objector says: "Some teachers maintain that there is no supreme self (*paramātman*) distinct from the body, the senses, the intellect, and so forth. Moreover—"
"The person is only as much as the range of the senses.
To this it is replied: there exists a self distinct from the body, the senses, the intellect, and so forth.
What is the illustration?
It is like a sword and its scabbard;
it is like the inner core of a reed. And it has been said:

Just as there is a distinction between a mosquito and an udumbara fruit, a blade of grass and muñja grass, a fish and water— despite their being one— the same applies, O King, to the field and the Self.

Thus, although the Supreme Self (paramātman) and the Person (puruṣa) have become unified with the body, senses, intellect, and so forth—like milk and water—they nevertheless exist as distinct from them.
Because they are subtle like primordial matter (pradhāna), they are not perceived; therefore, the means for their realization is stated:
