"Because composite objects exist for the sake of another, because of the reversal of the three qualities (guṇas) and so forth, and because of superintendence."
The Puruṣa exists because there must be an experiencer, and because of the activity directed toward the goal of isolation (kaivalya).
The Person exists, because composite things exist for the sake of another; for a composite thing exists for the sake of another.
For that reason:
in this world, whatever composite things are observed—such as beds, chariots, and shelters—are for the sake of another.
Likewise, the composite, the collection, of the limbs and the great elements (mahābhūtas) is also solely for the sake of another.
Therefore, there must certainly be something presiding over them, for the sake of which this aggregation exists; such is the connection.
For example, couches, chariots, and the like are aggregations of wood;
houses and the like are aggregations of wood, bricks, and so forth.
For these things— the chariot, the house, the couch, and so forth— do not accomplish any purpose of their own,
nor do they exist for one another's sake; rather, there exists that Devadatta or someone else who lies upon this couch, travels by means of the chariot, and dwells in the house.
(Conditioned by the mind:
Thus, these [elements] such as the great elements and the eye and so forth are neither for their own sake nor for one another's sake,
but rather for the sake of another.
And that which is the "other" is the self;
therefore, we infer that there exists a person for whose sake the aggregate of the eye and other faculties— the body— has arisen.
And for this reason [it exists]: because of the reversal of the three qualities and so forth.
That group in which the three qualities first arise is "the triad of qualities and so forth.
The reversal of that triad of qualities and so forth [proves its existence].
Therefore, we see that the Puruṣa exists.

In the preceding Āryā verse, it was stated that "possessing the three guṇas, non-discriminative," and so forth, which describes the common characteristics of the Manifest and Pradhāna; [it was also stated] that "the Puruṣa is the reverse of that, and likewise."
The existence and distinctness of the Self are established through the reversal of [the qualities of] the guṇas, non-discrimination, objectivity, generality, insentience, productivity,
and so forth. Furthermore, it exists because of its presiding over [the body].
For indeed, no collection of things exists without a presiding controller.
Just as in this world a chariot yoked with horses capable of leaping, swimming, and running proceeds only when presided over by a charioteer,
whereas if it were to proceed without being presided over by a charioteer, there would be the destruction of the body.
Nor does it act for the sake of its own destruction.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Ṣaṣṭitantra*: "Pradhāna proceeds when presided over by Puruṣa.
From this we see that there exists that Supreme Self, the Puruṣa, by whom Pradhāna is presided over so as to produce the Mahat, the Ahaṅkāra, the Tanmātras, the Indriyas, and the Bhūtas.
Therefore, the person exists. For this reason as well, he exists: because there must be an experiencer. Here, there are six tastes: sweet, sour, bitter, salty, pungent, and astringent.
Seeing food endowed with these six tastes, the eater is established:
"There exists an eater for whom this food belongs.

In the same way, seeing this manifest and unmanifest, we establish that there exists that Supreme Self, the Puruṣa, for whom this manifest and unmanifest is the object of enjoyment belonging to the eater.
For this reason as well, [the Pradhāna] exists: "And because of its activity for the sake of isolation.
Isolation (*kaivalya*) means the state of being alone, that is, liberation.
That activity of the Pradhāna is its activity for the sake of isolation. Thus ends verse 17.
Here the opponent says: "We have indeed accepted, on the basis of these five reasons studied, that this person exists as distinct from the body.
But is that person one and the same in all bodies, or is there a different person for each body?
If it is asked why there is such doubt, the respondent says: the doubt arises from the conflicting views of teachers."
In this regard, some teachers consider themselves proponents of non-duality (*abheda-vādin*), asserting: "This single Puruṣa is perceived in all bodies, like a thread through jewels.
Just as in this necklace, however many jewels there may be, a single thread runs through them all;
likewise, is there not one Supreme Self (*paramātman*) acting as the thread within these bodies that are like jewels?"
Or is it that the Puruṣa is like the moon in the water, perceived as one and the same in many places, such as rivers, wells, ponds, and so forth?
Therefore, there is a doubt: is there one Puruṣa according to the principle of the string of beads (*guṇasūtra*), or are there many Puruṣas?
To this it is replied: there are many Puruṣas. If it is asked how that is so, it is explained as follows:
The plurality of Puruṣas is established from the specific determination of birth, death, and the instruments [of action], from their non-simultaneous activity,
and also from the diversity of the three guṇas.
Regarding the phrase "of the causes of birth and death":
due to the determination of birth, some here are of low birth, while others are of middling birth.
Some are of superior birth.
If, however, there were only one person, he alone would be born into a low family and he alone would be born into a superior family. Why? Because of the oneness of the person.
And there is this rule: some are inferior and others are superior;
therefore, there are many persons.
And for this reason—because of the necessity of death; for even regarding death, a necessity is observed, as in: "My brother has died, my father has died.
Therefore, there are many persons.
Others, however, describe it in this way: because of the fixed order of birth and death.
Here, when one person dies at a certain time, another is born at that very same moment.
If there were but a single person, then when one is being born, everyone would be born as well.
But this is not the case; for if it were so, everyone would die simultaneously when one person dies,
yet this is not so.
Therefore, there are many Puruṣas. For this reason as well, we perceive [their plurality]:
because of the restriction of instruments.
The instruments are the sense faculties, such as hearing and the rest. In this world, some are deaf, blind, mute, and so forth, while others possess more acute faculties.
Therefore, we observe that those whose sense faculties are impaired are one set of people, while those whose sense faculties are unimpaired are another;
thus, because their instruments (the senses) are distinct, we also observe that there are many persons.
And for this reason as well, we see [it so]:
"and also because of the reversal of the three qualities.
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of conjunction.
By the reasons previously stated;
that is to say, for this reason. In this case, one Brāhmaṇa had three sons who were fellow-students (sabrahmacārin), all born of a single wife by a single [father].
Among them, one is of the nature of *sattva*: intelligent, pure, and happy; the second is of the nature of *rajas*: dull-witted and miserable;
the third is of the nature of *tamas*: deluded and a nihilist.
If there were but one Self, then when one person is characterized by sattva, rajas, or tamas, all would be so likewise;
yet they are not so.
Therefore, we perceive that there are many Puruṣas.
Here it is asked: this is the doubt.
Does the person (puruṣa) indeed exist as an agent, or rather as a non-agent?
If it is asked why there is this doubt:
This is due to the misconception regarding the teacher.
In the world, people hold the misconception that "a person walks," "he runs," "he stands," or "he grieves," and that "this was done by a person."
Thus the teachers who propound the Vedas speak; the Vaiśeṣikas also have adopted the view that there is a creator. Therefore, there is doubt.
To this it is replied: the Puruṣa is not an agent.
If it is asked how that is so, it is said:
from that very contrast, the witness-hood of this Puruṣa is established.
Isolation, neutrality, the state of being a witness, and the state of non-agency.
And regarding the phrase "from that perversion":
what is the distinction between an agent (*kartṛ*) and causes (*kāraṇa*)? To this it is said:
for example, there is a certain monk who dwells in a city, delighting in restraints and observances, and devoted to the teachers of Sāṅkhya and Yoga.
And he is merely a witness for the inhabitants of that city who engage in activities prescribed according to their respective castes and stages of life;
he experiences the cold, heat, and so forth that arrive by the power of the seasons.
In the same way, this Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), existing amidst the various states resulting from the conflict of the guṇas, would be a mere witness due to its dissimilarity [to them].
Thus, the witnesshood of this Puruṣa is established.
Kaivalya, known as the state of isolation, is the distinctness from the three guṇas.
It is just as that mendicant might sometimes become a speaker for citizens who are disputing, saying, "You have done well," or "You have not done well."
How does a person become thus?
To this it is said: [he attains] equanimity;
he has no business with anything whatsoever.
For this [Self] is indeed indifferent.
To this it is said: if it is a non-agent, then why is it the instigator of actions performed by others?
To this it is replied: for the state of being an agent is indeed twofold.
He is both the instigator and the agent;
here, the agency of the indifferent person is negated by the characteristic of the qualities (guṇas).

Here [the opponent] says: If the person (*puruṣa*) is not the agent, then what does he do when he forms a determination (*adhyavasāya*) such as "I shall perform merit" or "I shall perform demerit"? If the qualities (*guṇas*) perform the determination, then they would possess consciousness (*sacetanatva*);
yet, it was previously established that these [qualities] are indeed insentient (*acetanatva*).
If, on the other hand, the person were to exercise volitional determination (*adhyavasāya*), then it would follow that he possesses agency (*kartṛtva*).
Therefore, there is a fault in both cases.
To this, the following resolution is offered: this is not a fault.
If it is asked how this is so, it is said:
"Therefore, through union with that [Puruṣa], the insentient *liṅga* (the subtle body) appears as if it were sentient;
likewise, although the qualities (*guṇas*) are the actual agents, the indifferent [Puruṣa] appears as if he were the agent. (ISk 20)

Since the Puruṣa has consciousness as its inherent nature, therefore, through conjunction with it, the unconscious *liṅga*—consisting of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest—proceeds as if it were conscious in its functions, such as determination, self-conceit, volition, and perception.
What is the illustration? It is like this: for example, a jar that is neither hot nor cold becomes cold when touched by cold water.
Just as water becomes hot when conjoined with fire,
so too the subtle body (*liṅga*), though beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and being insentient, becomes as if possessed of consciousness.
Therefore, the *guṇas* perform the function of determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding effects and so forth.

As for what was said—that "the person (puruṣa) is the agent according to worldly convention"—to this we reply: even though the qualities (guṇas) are the agents, the indifferent one (udāsīna) appears as if he were the agent;
and here there is an illustration.

It is said that some thieves, having plundered a village and taken its wealth, were traveling toward another village having accomplished their task. A learned Brahmin was traveling along the same path with a caravan. Tracking their footprints, the guards seized them.

When those who have committed offenses seize that Brahmin as well, saying, "You too are a thief," then just as he— who is not a thief— is perceived as a thief by them due to the fault of association with them,
so too the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest are the agents; and the *puruṣa*, though joined with them and though himself a non-agent, becomes an agent.
Due to association with the agent, it appears as if it were an agent;
however, in the ultimate sense, the Puruṣa is not an agent.
Here it is asked: if it is argued that "from their conjunction" means the conjunction of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*, then what is this conjunction?
For conjunction is indeed of many kinds.
That produced by the action of one [of two things] is, for example, the conjunction between a post and a hawk; that produced by the collision of both is the conjunction of two fingers with space;
and that which is inherent is, for example, the conjunction between fire and heat.
An association caused by capacity is like that between a fish and water; a chance occurrence is like that between two *suparṇa* birds, being accidental.
Therefore, there is doubt.

To this it is replied: Conjunction produced by the action of either one is not possible in the case of the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa, because they are both all-pervading and inactive. Nor is there a natural conjunction;
since those two are eternal, there would be no liberation, as they could never be separated.
The same applies to [the cases] where the cause is the object and where the cause is the capacity.
To this, it is asked: "What then is the conjunction of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa)?
To this, it is said:
It is caused by a purpose.
And what is that purpose? To this he says: "For the sake of the Puruṣa’s seeing, and likewise for the sake of the Pradhāna’s isolation (kaivalya)."
The union of both is like that of the lame man and the blind man; from that [union] arises creation.
The conjunction of the Puruṣa is for the purpose of seeing;
the Puruṣa joins with Pradhāna with this intention: "I shall see Prakṛti, which possesses the [three] guṇas. Likewise, the conjunction of Pradhāna is for the purpose of liberation (kaivalya).

"I shall bring about liberation for this ascetic person who abides in knowledge"— liberation (kaivalya) meaning release (mokṣa). Just as a king unites with a man [thinking], "He will carry out my commands."
A man also associates with a king, thinking, "He will provide me with a livelihood.
In this way, first of all, the relationship between the king and the man is one caused by a purpose;
likewise, the conjunction—the relationship—between primordial matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa) is also caused by a purpose.
Furthermore, there is another point:
the conjunction of both is like that of the lame man and the blind man.
Moreover, there is an illustration for this.
It is said that once a certain blind man set out for Pāṭaliputra together with a caravan, and that caravan was attacked by bandits.
The blind man, his life still remaining, emerged with great difficulty.
Bereft of all his kinsmen and wandering here and there, he could not see the path; as he was pacing about, he was seen by a certain lame man staying in the middle of a forest, who spoke to him:
And he said: "O, O blind man, do not fear! I am lame; I am skilled at showing the way but unable to go.
The blind man replied: "O lame man, just as you are unable to go, so too am I unable to see."
"I have the capacity to go;
by means of your power of vision, I shall carry you on my shoulder and go. Thus, let there be the accomplishment of our purpose, characterized by the avoidance of suffering for both.
In this way, the connection between the two, which is a conjunction caused by the attainment of their respective self-interests, is equal.
In the same way,
the primary cause (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa) are to be viewed like the lame man and the blind man;
the spirit is to be viewed like the lame man.
Pradhāna is like a blind man;
the Puruṣa has the power of vision;
Pradhāna has the capacity for action.
In this way, Pradhāna also ceases its activity once it has accomplished the liberation of the Puruṣa;
having seen Pradhāna, the Puruṣa attains liberation. Furthermore: "Creation is brought about by that."

By that word, "the two" (tad), the primary matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa) are connected. Created by those two—the primary matter and the spirit—is the "creation produced by them" (tatkṛta-sarga).
For example: from the union of a woman and a man, a son is born.
Thus, from the conjunction of primary matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa), the production of creation occurs;
by the word "creation," they mean the arising of the subtle signs beginning with the Great Principle (mahat).
We shall explain that process of origination:

from primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the I-maker (ahaṅkāra); from that, the group of sixteen; and from five among that group of sixteen, the five gross elements arise. (ISk 22)
*Prakṛti*, *pradhāna*,
*avyakta*, *brahman*, *bahudhātmaka*, and *māyā* are synonyms. From that *prakṛti*, the "Great One" (*mahat*) arises as the first of all things.
Great, intellect, mind, wisdom.
consciousness, manifestation, and awareness.
Smṛti, Āsuri, Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha are synonyms.
From that [mahat] arises the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). From that mahat, the ego-sense is produced. Its synonyms are: vaikṛta, taijasa, bhūtādi, abhimāna, and asmitā.

Whatever is expressed by the sixty-four phonemes, ranging from Parā down to Vaikharī, once they have been mentally synthesized— that entire totality is designated as "Ahaṃkāra" (the I-maker) according to the method of *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation), being adorned with the *bindu* which resembles a globular mass situated above and which grasps the two phonemes *a* and *ha* at its beginning and end.
From that *ahaṃkāra*, the group of sixteen arises;
from the *tāmasa* *ahaṃkāra* known as *bhūtādi*, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) beginning with sound arise.
For this very reason, they are characterized as "deluded" (*mūḍha*).
From the *sāttvika* transformation known as *vaikṛta*, the eleven organs—consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and action (*karman*), together with the mind (*manas*)—arise.
For this very reason, they perceive something [external].
From the *rājasa* transformation known as *taijasa*, both [the internal and external] arise.
For darkness (tamas) is characterized by delusion, while goodness (sattva) is characterized by illumination;
from the ego (ahaṃkāra), the group of sixteen arises through the conjunction of these two qualities.
Therefore, from among those sixteen, from the five subtle elements (tanmātras) beginning with sound, the five gross elements beginning with space arise;
therein, from the subtle element of sound comes space,
and from the subtle element of touch comes air.
From the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra) comes fire; from the subtle element of taste (rasatanmātra) comes water;

and from the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra) comes earth. In this sequence, by the successive inclusion of each preceding element, the gross elements (mahābhūtas) ranging from ether to earth possess one, two, three, four, and five qualities respectively; such is the order of creation.
Therefore, it is "bha" because of the awakening to the arising and dissolution of the elements;
it is "ga" because of the thorough knowledge of coming and going; and it is "va" because the yogi knows [the truth].

It does not move excessively, thus it is *an*. From the tradition of all the phonemes (*varṇa*), the realization of the conceit "I am the Blessed One" (*bhagavān*) is established, even through the commonality of syllables and phonemes. (p. 27)
"One should explain [the etymology], but one need not respect the grammatical refinement" (Nirukti 2.4);
this is because of the authority of the Nirukta scripture. And it has been said:
"The origin and dissolution, as well as the coming and going of beings..."
"He who knows both knowledge and ignorance—he indeed is to be called Bhagavān."
In the sixth part of the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa (5.78), the words of Parāśara are as follows:
"That which was said..."
"Liberation is attained through the discernment of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower.
Among these, that which begins with the Great Principle (mahat) and ends with the gross elements has been explained as the "manifest.
The "unmanifest" is also [explained] by the verse: "Because of the finite measure of differentiated entities" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 15).
This has been explained by these five reasons. As it is said:

"One who knows the twenty-five principles, regardless of which stage of life he is devoted to—whether he has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot—is liberated; there is no doubt about this. (SkMv 22)
Here it is asked: it has been stated that "from primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat). What is the characteristic of that Great One? To this it is replied:
determination (adhyavasāya) is intellect (buddhi); [its specific qualities are] virtue (dharma), knowledge (jñāna), dispassion (virāga), and sovereignty (aiśvarya).
This form is characterized by sattva; that which is contrary to it is characterized by tamas.

"Intellect (buddhi) is determination (adhyavasāya). Determination means ascertainment or comprehension, such as "this is a post" or "this is a person"; this is the definition of intellect. And that intellect has eight aspects.
This is due to the distinction between the forms of *sāttvika* and *tāmasa*.
Among these, the *sāttvika* form of the intellect (*buddhi*) is fourfold: virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

Therein, what is called virtue (*dharma*) is that which is prescribed for those belonging to the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*) in accordance with their respective rules, characterized by the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*); that is virtue.
In that regard, there are five *yamas* and five *niyamas*.
"Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the *yamas*" (Pātañjala-yoga-sūtra 2.30).
"Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the *niyamas*" (Pātañjala-yoga-sūtra 2.32).
That which is accomplished by these restraints (yama) and observances (niyama) is Dharma.
Grammarians declare that the root *dhṛ* has the meaning of "holding.
It is called Dharma because it holds back living beings from falling into miserable states of existence.
In this context, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the absence of malice toward stationary and moving beings through the actions of speech, mind, and body.

Likewise, truth (*satya*) is that which is most beneficial to living beings; regarding objects perceived through direct observation, hearing, inference, or authoritative cognition, it is the utterance of speech that corresponds exactly to how they appear to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), without violating the senses and free from deception, error, or contradiction.
Likewise, when there is a cessation of grasping due to equanimity in one's respective places during other intense disturbances or extreme purposes, that is non-stealing (*asteya*).

Similarly, the avoidance of attachment in the union of male and female, in the mutual contact of sexual organs, and regarding sound, touch, taste, form, and smell; the cessation of the ear and other senses, as well as the lack of conceptualization and the cessation of the mind—that is the eightfold celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
For thus they say: celibacy (*brahmacarya*) consists of eight limbs, beginning with the renunciation of union, sound, touch, taste, form, smell, conceptualization, memory, and the fruits of merit.
Furthermore:
semen is the seed of *brahman*; he who moves about without emitting it is a *brahmacārī*.
It means one who practices the *brahman*—the Veda—bestowed by a teacher;
or, *brahmā* refers to the Self-Existent (*svayambhū*), and this [ascetic] practices in a manner like that of the *brahmā*, characterized by the carrying of the staff, water-pot, and so forth.

Thus, "non-possession" (*aparigraha*) is the non-acceptance of all things in every way, consisting in the non-undertaking of various conceptual constructions such as acquisition, buying, selling, and the like.

Thus are the five restraints (*yamāḥ*). That which is the cessation of the activity of the senses through the internal organ is inner purity (*śauca*); external purity is by means of earth, water, and so forth. Furthermore: "The avoidance of forbidden food, as well as not associating with those who are unfit..."
And remaining steadfast in one's own duty—this is proclaimed as purity.”
Likewise, one should perform the oblation into the internal fire with the mantra-empowered sacrificial offering obtained through alms; this moderation in food,
intended for the purpose of consuming the remnants of the sacrifice day after day, constitutes contentment.
“Whatever first oblation he should offer, [he should offer] ‘To Prāṇa, svāhā!

(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.19.1), beginning thus, up to: “He who, not knowing this, offers the Agnihotra—just as if one were to remove the embers and offer the oblation into the ashes, such would that [offering] be” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.3).
1) Thus says the Śruti.
Austerity (*tapas*) consists of practices such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, which take the form of emaciating the body. [As it is said:
"The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food."
As it is remembered [in the Bhagavadgītā 2.59]:
“For one who does not practice austerity, yoga is not perfected.”

Impurity, which is variegated by beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and consists of a web of present objects, cannot be dissolved without austerity; thus, the undertaking of austerity is prescribed. And they maintain that this should be practiced so as not to obstruct the clarity of the mind. Recitation (*svādhyāya*) is the chanting of the *praṇava* and other purifying mantras.
Devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) is the dedication of actions to the Supreme Teacher, or the renunciation of their fruits.
As it is said: “The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman” (Bhagavad Gītā 4.24), and “unattached to the fruit of action” (Bhagavad Gītā 6.1).
Because of such scriptural testimony,

from the practice of these restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth, there arise perfections (siddhis) such as that stated in the *Pātañjalayogaśāstra* (2.35): "When non-violence is firmly established, hostility ceases in his presence."
In the case of the opposite, however, there are the following [sūtras]: “When vitarka causes affliction, one should cultivate the counteractive measures” (Pātañjala-yoga-sūtra 2.33);

and “The counteractive cultivation is that [vitarkas] such as violence, whether committed, caused to be committed, or approved, being preceded by greed, anger, or delusion, result in endless fruits of suffering and ignorance” (Pātañjala-yoga-sūtra 2.34).

And for the yogin practicing in this manner, [there is the sūtra]: “Upon being invited by celestial beings, one should avoid attachment and pride, lest the undesirable consequence recur” (Pātañjala-yoga-sūtra 3.51).

51) Thus, these are the restraints and observances for a monk. It has been explained that the Dharma is accomplished by means of these restraints and observances. Now he speaks of knowledge: knowledge is of two kinds.
It is both external and internal.
Therein, the external consists of the lute, the drum, music, painting, storytelling, mathematics, and the treatises on grammar.
The internal is characterized by the perception of the distinction between the qualities (*guṇa*) and the person (*puruṣa*).
The qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are one thing, and the Puruṣa is another.
Worldly existence arises through external knowledge, while liberation arises through internal knowledge;
this knowledge results from the cessation of objective engagement with sense-objects.

He speaks of dispassion (*vairāgya*): for one who is detached from sense objects after perceiving the defects such as acquisition, preservation, loss, lack of contentment, and violence, there is no liberation.
Liberation occurs through internal dispassion preceded by knowledge, whereas through external [dispassion] there is worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).
Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) consists of the eightfold state of being a lord.

These are: *aṇimā* (minuteness), *laghimā* (lightness), *garimā* (heaviness), *mahimā* (greatness), *prāptiḥ* (attainment), *prākāmyam* (irresistible will), *īśitvam* (lordship), *vaśitvam* (control), and *yatrakāmāvasāyitvam* (the power to resolve at will).
These four qualities, beginning with *dharma*, are the forms of the intellect (*buddhi*) when it is characterized by *sattva*.
When *rajas* and *tamas* are overcome by *sattva*, then a person in whom *sattva* predominates attains these attributes.
Furthermore:
"The tamasic is the opposite of this.

The tamasic form of the intellect consists of the fourfold nature—unrighteousness, ignorance, and so forth—which is the reverse, that is, the opposite, of this aforementioned sattvic dharma and the rest.
For those discursive thoughts such as violence and so forth consist of eighty-one varieties;
likewise, the ten restraints (yama) and observances (niyama) are distinct.

Similarly, the intellect (buddhi) is eightfold through its divisions of sattva and tamas, namely: unrighteousness (adharma), ignorance (ajñāna), lack of dispassion (avairāgya), and lack of mastery (anaiśvarya).
From this kind of intellect, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) arises.
Now we shall explain the definition of *ahaṅkāra*. It is said:
"Ahaṅkāra is self-conceit; from it proceeds a twofold creation:
the elevenfold group of the senses and the fivefold group of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). (ISk 24)
Egotism is the conceit "I am":
"I am in form," "I am in taste," "I am in smell," "I am learned."
Ego (ahaṅkāra) is the conceit such as "I am handsome" and so forth.
From that ego, characterized by such conceit, a twofold creation proceeds.
"Creation" (sarga) is a synonym for "emanation" (sṛṣṭi).
And what is that creation? It is stated:
the elevenfold group of the senses;
the senses beginning with hearing and ending with the mind.
And also the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*);
here, the subtle elements are those beginning with sound and ending with smell.
Thus, the eleven sense organs and the five subtle elements have arisen.
Here it is asked: "The ego (ahaṅkāra) is threefold; we shall explain that.
Among these, from which ego do the sense organs arise, and from which do the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi) arise? To this it is replied:
The group of eleven, characterized by *sattva*, proceeds from the *vaikṛta* ego;
the subtle elements, characterized by *tamas*, proceed from the *bhūtādi*; and from the *taijasa*, both arise.
Regarding the term "sāttvika": when *sattva* is predominant within the *ahaṅkāra*, and by that *sattva* both *rajas* and *tamas* are overcome, then it is called the *sāttvika* *ahaṅkāra*.
The ancient teachers have given this *sāttvika* [type] the designation "vaikṛtika."
Becoming modified (*vaikṛtika*), that ego (*ahaṅkāra*) produces the eleven faculties.
Therefore, these [faculties] are characterized by *sattva*, being pure and capable of grasping their respective objects.
Hence it is said: "The group of eleven, characterized by *sattva*, proceeds from the modified ego."
From the *bhūtādi* [ego], the subtle elements arise.

From the *ahaṅkāra* named *bhūtādi*—which, due to the predominance of *tamas*, has rendered *sattva* and *rajas* subordinate—as described by the former teachers, the group of five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), beginning with sound, is born.

From the *rājasa* *ahaṅkāra* known as *taijasa*, in which *sattva* and *tamas* are suppressed, both [classes] arise from the activity of *pravṛtti*: namely, the eleven organs, which are of the nature of illumination, and the subtle elements, which are of the nature of delusion.
This is the connection [of the words].
Only in the *rājasa* ego (*ahaṅkāra*), which is of the nature of fire (*taijasa*), does the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) exist.
*Sattva*, being inactive and solitary, is not able to produce [effects] on its own.
And because it is characterized by delusion (*mūḍhatva*), *tamas* is inactive and incapable of producing creation without *rajas*.

Therefore, the intended meaning is that both *sattva* and *tamas*, when assisted by *rajas* regarding the matter of creation, generate the two groups consisting of the sense organs (*aindriyaka*) and the subtle elements (*tānmātrika*).
In this regard, which are the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) and which are the organs of action (*karmendriya*)? It is said:
the sense organs of cognition are known as the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose;
they call the voice, hands, feet, anus, and genitals the organs of action. (ISk 26)
The ears and so forth are called the sense-faculties of cognition (*buddhīndriya*).
They are called sense-faculties of cognition because they cognize sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
These very faculties are the sense-faculties.
The word *in* is a name for objects (*viṣaya*); because they run toward those objects, they are called *indriya*s (senses).
Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ are said to be the organs of action (*karmendriya*).
They perform actions and cause them to be performed; this is the function of the organs of action (*karmendriya*). Speech is the action of speaking.
The two hands perform the action of grasping;
the two feet traverse uneven and even ground, as well as places that are low and high; and the anus expels the waste of food and water as it has been consumed.
The generative organ produces bliss; the meaning is that it brings about the birth of a son.
Thus have these functions of the organs of action been explained.

Here it is asked: "What is the characteristic of that sense-organ, the mind? To this it is replied: "In this context, the mind is of a dual nature; it is both the faculty of volition (*saṅkalpaka*) and a sense-organ (*indriya*) due to its common properties.
Its diversity arises from the specific transformations of the *guṇas* and from the distinction between its objects of perception. (ISk 27)
In this context, the mind possesses a dual nature:
it is a faculty of action among the organs of action,
and a faculty of cognition among the organs of cognition.

Just as Devadatta, standing among cowherds, performs the duties of a cowherd, and standing among wrestlers, performs the duties of a wrestler—why is this? Because he conceives the activity of both the cognitive organs (*buddhīndriya*) and the organs of action (*karmendriya*).
Therefore, the mind (*manas*) is of a dual nature.
Furthermore:
"And the faculty [is so called] because of its commonality.
Commonality (sādharmya) is the state of having a shared property (sahadharmasya bhāvaḥ).
Since the organs of action and the organs of perception arise from the sattvic ego,
the mind also arises from that very same source;
therefore, the mind is an organ.
In that regard, what is the function of the mind?
Its function is volition (saṅkalpa). The functions of the sense organs of cognition are sound and the other objects of perception.
The functions of the organs of action are speech and so forth.
Thus, the eleven organs have been explained together with their functions.
Here one asks: "By whom were these eleven organs created—by the Puruṣa, by Īśvara, or by inherent nature (svabhāva)? If it is asked why this doubt arises:
These eleven faculties are the perceivers of the eleven objects.
Among them, the internal instruments—the primary intellect (*buddhi*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth—are insentient.
Therefore, they must necessarily be directed by a sentient agent, whether that be the *puruṣa*, the Lord (*īśvara*), or inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
To this it is replied: their diversity arises from the specific transformations of the *guṇas* and from the difference in their respective objects.
The three *guṇas*, beginning with *sattva*, transform in various ways; from these specific transformations of the *guṇas*, these eleven sense organs are diverse, and their objects are distinct.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell belong to the five [senses]; speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure belong to the five [action organs];
and volition belongs to the mind.
Of these very eleven, the sense-faculties (*indriya*) will be the apprehenders.

Furthermore, this diversity is not created by Īśvara, nor by intellect (*buddhi*), nor by ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), nor by primordial matter (*pradhāna*), nor by the person (*puruṣa*), nor by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
rather, it is produced through the transformation of the qualities (*guṇapariṇāma*).
Although it was stated that the activity of insentient *guṇas* is illogical,
that is not so.
If one asks why, it is said in response:
The activity of even insentient things is observed;
for it will be said:
"Just as the flow of milk, though insentient, occurs for the sake of the growth of the calf."
"The activity of the Pradhāna proceeds in this way for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa."
(Sāṅkhyakārikā 57).
Therefore, even though the *guṇas* are insentient, they undergo transformation into the state of the eleven organs.
Here it is asked: "We grant for now that the eleven organs are produced from the *ahaṃkāra*."
By whom was the placement of these sense-faculties according to their respective locations determined?
[It was so that] the eye would be situated high up, capable of seeing at a distance;
and the ear would be situated in the region of the head, capable of hearing from afar.

The skin is situated both inside and outside the body and will be capable of perceiving various types of touch; the tongue is situated within the mouth and will be capable of perceiving various tastes;
likewise for the nose and the voice.
Thus, it may be asked whether the deployment of the sense faculties was performed by a person (*puruṣa*), or by a Lord (*īśvara*), or by inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
To this it is replied: here in the Sāṅkhya system, neither the person, nor the Lord, nor inherent nature is the cause.
What then? The deployment was performed by the three qualities (*guṇa*)—sattva, rajas, and tamas—residing within this ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
Therefore, we say: "The diversity [of the senses] arises from the specific transformations of the *guṇas* and from the difference in their objects.
The distinction among the eleven organs results from the specific transformations of the *guṇas*, and also from the difference in their respective objects.
The objects of the eleven faculties are to be grasped; from their differentiation, there is also a differentiation of the faculties.

Here it is asked: what is the function (vṛtti) of which [faculty]? It is said: with respect to form and the other [objects], the mere observation (ālocana-mātra) is held to be the function of the five [sensory faculties].
But speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure are the functions of the five [motor faculties]. (ISk 28)
The word *mātra* signifies "only" or "nothing but.
Just as when one receives only alms and no other special gift,
so it is with the eye.
Regarding the phrase "merely a perception of what has already been reached":
each sense organ possesses the capacity to grasp its own respective object;
for the eye is not capable of hearing, nor is it capable of giving or taking.
Henceforth, we shall explain the functions of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*). It is said:
"The function of the triad [of these] is specific to its own characteristics; this is their uncommon [function].
The function common to the instruments [of perception and action] consists of the five vital airs, beginning with *prāṇa*. (ISk 29)
Regarding the term "specific characteristic" (*svālakṣaṇya*):
the definition of the intellect (*buddhi*) was previously stated as "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*). That very ascertainment is its function (*vṛtti*).
Thus, conceit is the defining characteristic of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra);
its function is that very same thing.
The defining characteristic of the mind (manas) is volition (saṅkalpa).
Its function is also that very same one;
by whichever characteristic these are characterized, that indeed is their function.
Thus, that which is the function of the sense organs is not the function of the organs of action.
That which is the function of the organs of action is not the function of the organs of perception;
the functions of the intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and mind (manas) have been described,
and they too are specific (asāmānya).

Characterized by determination, self-conceit, and volition, this [function] is "not common," meaning it is unique. When it is stated thus, it is understood by implication that there is also a function that is "common" or shared;
it is in relation to that [common function] that it is called "not common."
Thus has been described the specific function of the organs, which is comparable to that of a woman of good family.
Hereafter, their common function is stated:
the common function of the organs consists of the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa.

The "common function of the organs" (sāmānyakaraṇavṛtti) means the function of the internal organ as a whole. The five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa—namely prāṇa, apāna, udāna, samāna, and vyāna—perform a common function for all the sense organs.
That which moves within the mouth and nose and has its activity directed toward external objects is called prāṇa.

Because it causes breathing, this is designated as "prāṇa. Regarding the question of by whom that activity of vibration within this *prāṇa* is performed, it is stated here: it is performed by the thirteenfold instrument (*karaṇa*).
And since this is so, therefore the activity of *prāṇa* is the common function of the entire collection of instruments.
Moreover, there is an illustration for this: suppose there are parrots living in a cage in a certain royal palace.
When Devadatta showed them some boiled rice, upon seeing the rice, they all began to move about.
Then the cage also moved;
just as that action of the cage’s movement was common to all the parrots,
so too that action of vibration in the vital breath (prāṇa) is common to all the sense organs.
Furthermore: it emits by means of the *apāna*.
Because of this departure from here, it is called *apāna*.
And Devadatta, being full of *apāna*, retreats upon seeing a snake; this is *apāna*.
In that *apāna*, the activity of vibration is the common function (*sāmānyavṛtti*) of all the sense organs.
When there is an upward movement resulting in the elevation of objects, it is designated as *udāna*;
it rises from the region of the navel and moves upward.

And the function of *udāna* is that Devadatta seeks an increase in joy, thinking, "I am wealthy; how might I become wealthier than this? This is *udāna*. Within this *udāna*, the activity of vibration is the common function of all the sense faculties.
Furthermore: its abiding in the heart and its coexistence with that [fire] are common to it.
That wind which operates in the region of the heart is the *samāna*;
and because it abounds in that [fire], it does not delight in being alone—this is the *samāna*.
In that [vital air], the activity of vibration is the common function (*sāmānyavṛtti*) of all the sense organs.
Furthermore, it is called *vyāna* because it pervades the body;
since it pervades the body from the nails to the tips of the hair and moves without [excessive] fluctuation, it is called *vyāna*.
And Devadatta, who is abundant in *vyāna*, finds pleasure entirely without another.
That activity of vibration which exists in that *vyāna* is the common function (*sāmānyavṛtti*) of all the sense-faculties.
Thus, the vital airs beginning with *prāṇa* have been explained as having the function of being common causes.
We shall explain the functioning [of the senses]. It is said:
"The functioning of the fourfold [set] is indeed simultaneous and also sequential;
likewise, when the object is perceived, and when it is unperceived, the functioning of the triad is preceded by that. (ISk 30)
Intellect, ego-sense, mind, and the eye— these four perceive a form simultaneously,
[determining] "this is a post" or "this is a person.
In the same way, these four grasp sound, touch, taste, and smell simultaneously.

Thus, this is the simultaneous operation of the fourfold group. Furthermore, its sequential operation is also specified: the operation of that fourfold group—intellect, ego-sense, mind, and eye—occurs in succession.

Because the instruction regarding the distinction between door and doorway occurs over a very short period of time, that distinction cannot be described; therefore, it is said to be "simultaneous," just as when it is said that a hundred lotus petals have been pierced by the point of a needle.
For example:
Devadatta, while walking along a path, sees a post; there, a doubt arises in him as to whether this is a post or a person.
There he perceives the form of a post and a bird perched upon it, whereupon the cognition arises in him, "This is a post.
He then performs the actions of contracting and extending [his limbs], and from that too comes the realization, "This is a person."
In this way, the sequential functioning of the intellect, ego, mind, and eye is observed: the eye sees form,
the mind conceives,
and the ego conceives of itself [as the agent].
The intellect determines;
the same should be understood for the tongue and the other senses as well.
Furthermore: "Whether [the object] is seen or likewise unseen."
The functioning of the triad is preceded by that;
by the word "that," the sense-faculties just mentioned are meant.
Regarding form, it is preceded by the eye.
In the case of sound, it is preceded by the ear; in the case of touch, by the skin; in the case of taste, by the tongue.
Regarding odor, the activity of the intellect, ego, and mind is preceded by the sense of smell.
To this, he says: "By what cause do the insentient sense organs, intellect, ego, and mind each undertake their respective functions? To this, he replies:
"They undertake their respective functions caused by mutual intention.
The purpose of the Puruṣa alone is the cause; no instrument is set in motion by anyone else. (ISk 31)
They maintain that the term *svāṃ svām* expresses repetition (*vīpsā*).
(Thus, the inclusion of the thirteenfold instrument is accomplished.
The meaning is that they "attain" or "grasp."
Furthermore: their functioning is caused by mutual intentionality.
Having perceived the intention of the intellect (buddhi), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) conceives pride;
the mind (manas) forms volitions.
The sense faculties each engage in their respective functions. *Ākūta* means intention (*abhiprāya*).
For example, it is said that when a band of thieves goes to plunder a village, there is a signal given by the leader of the thieves. (p. 35)
It was arranged that whenever I say "Hā! Hā!", everyone must enter together; but whenever I say "Ahā! Hā!", then they must exit.
Having understood this command and the intention of the bandit chief, the thieves entered and exited accordingly.
Likewise, in this case, the intellect (*buddhi*) stands in the place of the commander of a band of thieves, while the sense faculties (*indriya*) stand in the place of the thieves.
Whether they apprehend their objects for their own sake or for the sake of another is what is now addressed:
it is understood that they act for the sake of another.
For it has been said: "The purpose of the Puruṣa alone is the cause; the activity of the Guṇas proceeds only because the purpose of the Puruṣa must be accomplished.
Therefore, this thirteenfold instrument is set in motion by the purpose of the Puruṣa.
As for what was also asked—"How do the instruments, being insentient, proceed?"—[the answer follows].
To this we reply: no instrument is caused by anything—not by Īśvara, nor even by Puruṣa.
There is no such thing as "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) that exists as a distinct entity.
For it is because the thirteenfold instrument itself operates within its own respective objects.
Here it is asked: It has been stated by the Blessed One that "no instrument is caused [to act] by anything.
Therefore, how many kinds of instruments are there? To this it is replied:
The instrument is of thirteen kinds; it performs the functions of grasping, supporting, and manifesting.
And its function is tenfold: it is to be taken up, maintained, and revealed.
It should be understood that what is called "the instruments" (karaṇa) here is of thirteen kinds:
the five organs of action (karmendriya) and the five organs of cognition (buddhīndriya).
Intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*)—these constitute the thirteenfold instrument (*karaṇa*).
Regarding this, it is said: "It is the appropriator (*āhāraka*), the sustainer (*dhāraka*), and the illuminator (*prakāśaka*).
Among these, that which is characterized by the sense organs (*indriya*) is the appropriator.
The characteristic of the *ahaṃkāra* (the I-maker) is retention;
the characteristic of *buddhi* (intellect) is illumination.
Here it is asked: does that [entity] exist for which the acts of taking up, retaining, and illuminating are performed?
To this it is replied: its effect is tenfold—namely, that which is to be grasped (*āhārya*), that which is to be maintained (*dhārya*), and that which is to be manifested (*prakāśya*).
"Effect" (*kārya*) refers to the five [objects]: sound, touch, taste, form, and smell; and the five [actions]: speaking, taking, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure.
These ten objects are called the "task.
The organs of action take up and sustain that tenfold object— the matter revealed by the sense organs—
just as one takes up and holds with the hand a jar situated in the dark that has been illuminated by a lamp.
Thus, just as it is with the jar, so it is with all the remaining [elements] as well.
The internal organ is threefold, while the external is tenfold; it is called the "object" of the triad.
The external organ functions in the present time, whereas the internal organ functions in all three times.

"The internal organ is threefold" refers to the apprehension of the intellect (*buddhi*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and the mind (*manas*). These three are designated as the "internal organs. The external [organs] are tenfold, due to the distinction between the organs of cognition and the organs of action.
Furthermore:

the tenfold external instrument known as the objects of the three— namely, the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*)— is the external instrument called "object" belonging to these three internal instruments.
"Enjoyable" means that the internal triad consists of the masters, while the external tenfold group consists of the servants;
furthermore, the external is for the present time.
This external tenfold instrument that has been described functions with respect to the present time, grasping objects that are currently existing.
The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose grasp only present sounds and so forth; they do not grasp those that are past nor those that are yet to come.

In this way, speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ function with respect to present objects—namely, speaking, grasping, walking, excreting waste, and experiencing pleasure—but not with respect to the past or the future.
Furthermore, the internal instrument consisting of the mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*) operates across the three periods of time.
The intellect perceives a present jar, and it also remembers those that are past or will be in the future.

For example: Yudhiṣṭhira and Bhīmasena represent the intellect that grasps past objects; Kalkī represents the intellect that will grasp future things. In this same way, the ego (ahaṅkāra) also pertains to all three times.
Just as I was the master in this house and shall be [the master] again,
so too the mind conceptualizes the past, the present, and the future.
Since this is so, it is therefore said: "The internal instrument [functions] throughout the three times."
Here it is asked: which sense organs perceive their objects with specific qualities (*saviśeṣa*), and which perceive them without specific qualities (*nirviśeṣa*)? To this it is replied:
among the sense organs, five have as their objects both the specific and the non-specific.
Speech has sound as its object, and the remaining [faculties] also have the five objects [as their domain].

Among those organs, those of which this [treatment] applies—namely, the five sense organs of cognition (buddhīndriya), viz., hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell—they perceive their objects both with distinctions (saviśeṣa) and without distinctions (aviśeṣa). Here it is asked: for which [organ] do they perceive the object with distinctions, and for which without distinctions?

To this it is replied: sound, touch, taste, form, and smell are called the *tanmātras* (subtle elements) of the five deities; they are without distinction because they consist solely of the characteristic of pleasure.
Since neither suffering nor delusion exists therein, they are therefore without distinction. For instance:

They are "with distinctions" (*saviśeṣa*) because they are distinguished by qualities such as being peaceful, terrible, or deluded; "without distinctions" (*nirviśeṣa*) means they are devoid of such [qualities].
This is the intended meaning: likewise, for human beings, sound and the other objects are "with distinctions," meaning they are associated with pleasure, pain, and delusion.
In the case of the gods, however, the sense organs of cognition manifest exclusively as consisting of pleasure.
The sense organs of cognition for both gods and humans have been described;
we shall now speak of the organs of action.
Speech has sound as its object, as do the remaining five objects. In that regard, the speech of the gods utters a quarter-verse, a half-verse, or a complete verse; ours is exactly the same.
Therefore, the meaning is that the faculty of speech is equal for both us and the gods.
Furthermore: "The remaining five objects as well.
Of those four [faculties], each one has five objects.
The hand is endowed with sound, touch, taste, form, and smell; thus,
the tactile faculty (*pāṇīndriya*), possessing these five characteristics when in proximity, grasps a pot that likewise possesses five characteristics—
since both the hand and the tactile faculty possess these five characteristics.
Thus, the foot, characterized by the five [objects] beginning with sound, moves only upon the ground which consists of five [elements].
Likewise, the anus and the genitals, though characterized by five [elements], perform the two functions of excretion and pleasure, each characterized by five.
Therefore, it is rightly said: "The remaining five are also objects."
Now, this is stated in order to demonstrate that the object of cognition is the intellect (buddhi):
"Since the intellect, together with the internal organs, penetrates every object, therefore the threefold instrument is the gatekeeper, while the remaining ones are the gates. (ISk 35)

"Accompanied by the internal organ" (*sāntaḥkaraṇā*) means that which exists together with the internal organ— that is, the intellect (*buddhi*) along with the "I-sense" (*ahaṃkāra*) and the mind (*manas*).
Because that intellect penetrates, pervades, and grasps every object without exception throughout all three times—
namely, the fivefold objects beginning with sound— it is for that very reason threefold, characterized as mind, intellect, and the "I-sense."
Thus, the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the means (*sādhana*), because it is by means of this that [an action] is performed.
Furthermore, the remaining ones— which are known as the organs of cognition and action, such as the ear, speech, and so forth— are external to the door.

These ten are merely the gateways or instruments for that very intellect (*buddhi*), which is joined with the mind (*manas*) and ego (*ahaṅkāra*), for the purpose of grasping objects; they are not inherently connected to it as functional organs (*karaṇa*).
Thus, the meaning is that through these ten gateways, the intellect itself—along with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—grasps the objects; therefore, the instrument is indeed threefold.
Furthermore:
These specific qualities, which are like lamps and distinct from one another, having illuminated the entire object of the Puruṣa, present it to the intellect. (ISk 36)
"These" refers to the thirteen distinctions of the intellect, the organs of action, and the internal organ; they are like lamps, that is, equal to lamps.
Furthermore, they are mutually distinct from one another.
"Having different characteristics" means they are dissimilar;
for the ear perceives sound, but not touch and the other [objects].
The same applies elsewhere:
speech indeed speaks, but it does not grasp, it goes, it dwells, or it rejoices;
the same is true for the hand and the other [limbs].
The mind (manas) forms volitions (saṅkalpayati) but does not exercise egoism (ahaṅkurute);
and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) conceives self-identification (abhimanute) but does not form volitions.
Thus, all twelve [faculties], having manifested their respective objects as things to be enjoyed by the Puruṣa, present them to and deposit them within the intellect (buddhi).
The Puruṣa perceives that object—pleasure, pain, and so forth—which resides within the intellect (buddhi).
Furthermore:

Since the intellect accomplishes every object of experience for the Puruṣa, and since it alone distinguishes [the objects], it therefore discerns the subtle difference between Pradhāna and Puruṣa. (ISk 37)

Because, with respect to the objects of experience in all three times, whatever enjoyment occurs for a person— whether among gods or in the animal realm— it is *buddhi* alone that accomplishes and brings it about for him,
like a king’s minister. Just as a minister, having arranged the affairs of all his servants, reports them to the king.
In this way, having illuminated the objects, the organs of action deliver them to the intellect;
the intellect, in turn, delivers and presents them to the Puruṣa.
In this manner, the intellect [is connected] with the fruit of worldly prosperity.
As long as knowledge does not arise, it binds the person, just as a wanton woman binds a lover; thus, deluded consciousness is bound by the offerings of ghee and other such things.

Impelled by the intellect (*buddhi*), that which is called the ego, mind, intellect, and organs of action accomplish objects not for their own sake, nor for the sake of the intellect, but solely for the sake of the Person (*puruṣārtha*).

Just as in the house of a woman who lives by her own will and possesses wealth, the female servants prepare the flavorful food not for themselves, nor for the sake of the mistress who dwells there as their owner, but rather for the sake of the lover whose discrimination and discernment have been stolen away by her;
so long as that man remains deluded, he is led away by the objects of the senses by this very intelligence, which is like that mistress.

When he somehow becomes conscious of the self through the teacher, the scriptures, and personal experience, then even the intellect, like a wanton woman, ceases its activity upon abandoning the person.
Thereafter, he remains in a state of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*). To claim that liberation is the continued existence in that experience is merely some irrelevant matter.
The present subject is stated:
furthermore,
for this reason, that very [intellect] distinguishes the subtle difference between the primary matter (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa).
It is subtle and difficult to discern;
it is the distinction and diversity between the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa.
This means that because of its subtlety, it is exceedingly hard to understand.
For the intellect (*buddhi*), whose nature is determination (*adhyavasāya*), accomplishes [its task] through its own function, which is determination.

Having distinguished the world through the determination of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the senses, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the gross elements, and having distinguished it by discerning the difference between primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*), it itself ceases.
Therefore it has been said:
The ego says to the intellect: "Do not awaken this one who is asleep. For when supreme bliss is awakened, there is neither you, nor I, nor that world.
While I, the ego-principle, remain present, how can the twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa, desire liberation after having abandoned the multitude of the principles?
"That God who is the Lord of All, all-pervading, and the Teacher of the World—
by uttering the word 'dehī' (embodied), alas, I have made that Self appear small!"
The distinction between Pradhāna and Puruṣa cannot be attained by those who have not performed meritorious deeds. He shows the difference between these two:
you do not know yourself as distinct [from it].

Pradhāna is something else. The three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are the constituents of Pradhāna; they are formless and, in a state of equilibrium, are designated as Pradhāna. From their unity and from the predominance [of one over the others], another entity arises: the intellect (buddhi), which consists of the three qualities.
Having understood that the ego-sense is one thing, the five subtle elements are another,
and the eleven organs are yet others, those who know the principles attain liberation.
Indeed, in the system of the Blessed Kapila, there is nothing whatsoever to be performed as a duty;

rather, for the Sāṅkhyas, the knowledge of the twenty-five principles alone—both through their similarities and their differences—is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). And it has been said:
Laugh, drink, sport, and rejoice eternally; enjoy the objects of the senses and harbor no fear.
If you have understood the doctrine of Kapila, then you shall attain the bliss of liberation.
Here it is asked: It was stated by the Blessed One in the preceding verse that "the sense organs have as their objects both the specific and the non-specific.
In that regard, what are the specifics and what are the non-specific? To this it is replied:
The subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are the non-specific; from those five [subtle elements] arise the five gross elements (*bhūta*).
These are remembered as the specific states—quiescent, terrible, and deluded.
Those five subtle elements (tanmātras), beginning with sound, which arise from the tamasic ego characterized by the notion of "the elements" (bhūtādi), are called "non-specific" (aviśeṣa).

For the gods, these subtle elements are objects characterized by pleasure; yet even there, rajas and tamas exist, though sattva prevails in its intensity. Therefore, they are called "non-specific. The meaning is that they do not differ [from one another] due to the predominance of sattva, existing solely as pleasure, and thus lack distinctions such as being peaceful, terrible, or delusive.

What, then, are the specific qualities (viśeṣas)? To this he says: "From those, the five elements [arise]; from the five, beginning with sound. From the five [qualities], beginning with sound, the five great elements—ether and the rest—arise, possessing one, two, three, four, and five qualities respectively, due to the successive penetration of each preceding element into the next.
These are known as the specific qualities (viśeṣas).
Here it is asked: what is the definition of these?
To this it is replied:
These five great elements are the objects of human beings;
they are peaceful, terrible, and delusive.
Among them, space is peaceful, terrible, and delusive.
First, that which is characterized by pleasure is peaceful (*śānta*).
For example, someone who has emerged from an inner chamber and stands in the open air would find that space to be peaceful because it is a cause of pleasure;
yet that very same space would become terrible (*ghora*) due to suffering caused by contact with heat, cold, wind, and so forth.
For a man traveling on a road who is fleeing in fear, seeing only empty space everywhere and being ignorant of the path and so forth, that very [space] would be a source of delusion.
In the same way, there is a threefold nature in the wind:
just as for one staying in an inner chamber, the wind entering through the window is "calm" because it is a cause of pleasure.
Because that very heat, when fully developed, produces suffering, one would be miserable; thus, that wind is "terrible.
That same wind, producing cold during the cold season, is "deluded.
Likewise, fire is "appeased" for one afflicted by cold.

In the summer season, fire is "terrible" to one afflicted by heat; when it has intensified during a village conflagration or similar event, it is "deluded" because it produces delusion in a person. Likewise, water is "peaceful" because it provides comfort to one distressed by the heat.
The winter seasons are "terrible" because they give rise to suffering;
they are "delusive" because they cause confusion in a man who has gone out to sea and cannot see the shore.
Likewise, the earth, covered with fresh grass in the rainy season, is "peaceful" because it brings happiness.
In the summer season, the hot sands are terrible;
they are likewise bewildering for a traveler who does not know the way and perceives no villages or living beings.
In this same way, the sense objects of the gods are devoid of any distinction.

Known as the *tanmātras*, they are devoid of distinctions, consisting of pure bliss, and undifferentiated by being peaceful, terrible, or deluded; they are of the nature of their own essence (*svabhāva-rūpa*), like sugar, pungent, or bitter tastes which are certainly nectar-sweetness in their essential nature, or like milk which possesses the happiness of its own quality,
or like water whose natural taste is conjoined with earthly qualities such as sweetness, alkalinity, or pungency— such are these objects (*viṣaya*).
In this way, they would be indistinguishable from the gods, being designated as mere [objects of] that [pleasure] and characterized solely by happiness.

For humans, however, because they are composed of the elements such as space and so forth, they possess the characteristics of pleasure, pain, and delusion like the elements themselves; this is the meaning.
Here he asks: Are the objects of cognition limited to just these? No;
rather, there are others as well.
But what are they? It is said:
The subtle [beings], those born of parents, and those together with the gross—these are the three types of distinctions.
Among them, the subtle are constant, while those born of parents cease.
In that regard, first, there are the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*). By means of these very [elements], the subtle bodies of all three worlds were initiated at the original creation.
That subtle body enters the mother's womb at the time of conception;
[it consists of] the mother’s blood and the father’s semen.
The proponents of Vedānta also say this:
living beings, after experiencing the fruits of their own karma in the heavens, hells, and other realms, desire to return here; having become merged into the lunar orb, they become rain.
From that comes food, which, when consumed by a man and a woman, becomes semen and blood.
Then [it asks], "Do you know how, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3), beginning with which it concludes, "Thus, at the fifth oblation, the waters...
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.9).
1) Thus they say. Also in the Purāṇas: "Soma, rain, food, and semen—the person is the fifth therein."
"He lives for Agni; they carry him away from where he arose."
Thus, it brings about the growth of the subtle body.
The essence of the food and drink consumed by the mother, having entered through connection with the mother's channels, effects the growth of the subtle body composed of semen and blood.
And it enters the umbilical opening of the infant from the mother's vessel;
just as water, through a single channel, provides nourishment to a vegetable garden, so too the essence of food and drink, having entered the mother's vessel, enters the infant's navel.
Having entered, it provides nourishment to the infant's body.
In that regard, the configuration of the subtle body possesses the same characteristics as the external body, namely: hands, feet, head, back, belly, shanks, and ankles.
Furthermore, the learned say that the external body consists of six sheaths (*ṣāṭkauśika*):
blood, flesh, and skin are born from the mother; sinews, bones, and marrow are born from the father.
Thus, this external body brings about the nourishment of the internal subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*).

At the time of birth, when that very subtle body— which has been nourished by the external body— emerges from the mother’s womb through the birth canal, the five external great elements (*mahābhūta*), beginning with earth, are made to serve as its support and basis for movement.
Just as for a certain prince who has been nurtured by his parents, the five great elements have been prepared:
space for providing room, and earth for walking upon.
Water is for the formation of the body and for purification; fire is for the digestion of food;
wind is for distribution.
Thus, these three kinds of specific constituents of this very body are subtle, those born of the mother and father, and those that are abundant;
"pra" is a prefix.
Thus, the meaning is that the elements derived from mother and father are subtle;
these are the [elements] such as earth and so forth.
In this way, these are the threefold distinctions.

And as for the other specific qualities previously mentioned—namely, the peaceful, the terrible, and the deluded—it is asked here: "Among these three types of specific qualities, which are eternal and which are non-eternal? To this it is replied: "The subtle ones among them are fixed. "Subtle" refers to those by which the commencement of the initial creation occurs; "fixed" means eternal.

The subtle body initiated by those [karmas] falls into this gross body; joined with demerit (adharma), it perceives the five states ending with domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and immobile beings.
Through the equilibrium of merit and demerit, it perceives the states beginning with Brahmins and ending with Caṇḍālas.
Thus, the meaning is that the subtle body is constant throughout the cycle of transmigration (saṃsāra).
Thus, as long as that knowledge—which consists in the perception of the distinction between the qualities (*guṇas*) and the person (*puruṣa*)—has not arisen, one transmigrates;
once that knowledge has arisen, [transmigration] ceases.
And when that has ceased, the person attains liberation. As it has been said:

“When the body, which is the locus of delusion, has been dissolved, he becomes united with the Supreme Self and attains a state of oneness, like the space within a jar merging with the universal space.”
“As when there is an absence of a mirror, there is the disappearance of the reflection,” and so forth.
Therefore, this [subtle body] is subtle.
Those born of mother and father cease; having abandoned that subtle body at the time of death, the one born of mother and father falls away.
That subtle body transmigrates for those who lack knowledge.

Here it is said: The Blessed One has stated, "Those born of mother and father cease; that which is subtle transmigrates"—this is the meaning. To this, it is replied: "The *liṅga* (the subtle body), which arose previously, is unattached, determinate, and extends from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the subtle elements; devoid of sensory enjoyment, it transmigrates, being permeated by dispositions (*bhāva*). (ISk 40)
"Arisen previously," and so forth;
the meaning is "arisen at the beginning of creation.
The meaning is that as long as knowledge has not arisen, one remains very firmly established in saṃsāra.
Furthermore: "unattached" (asakta) means not attached anywhere; because of its subtlety, it is unattached among gods, humans, and animals.
"Fixed" (niyata) means eternal (nitya).

The five organs of action, the five organs of cognition, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*)—thus there are eighteen: from the Great One (*mahat*) down to the subtle [elements].
This is described as that which has "the Great One" at its beginning and the "subtle elements"—known as the objects such as sound and so forth—at its end.
The thirteen organs—consisting of the internal organs and the external organs—and the five subtle elements (tanmātras).
To this, he asks: "What does that do?
To this it is replied: "It transmigrates through the wombs of gods, humans, and animals; it assumes the state of a living being."
For that [puruṣa] is devoid of experience; the objects such as sound are the experiences, and it is devoid of them.
The meaning is that it consists solely of the thirteen instruments.
It is "perfumed by states of being" (bhāva-adhivāsita); the meaning is that it is indeed perfumed by the states of being of gods, humans, and animals.
Just as [perfuming occurs] like sesame seeds, a cloth, or a dwelling,
so too do entities become pacified:
divine states through the auspicious, human states through the mixed, and the state of animals through the inauspicious.
It is called *liṅga* because at the time of dissolution it goes to dissolution (*laya*) within the *pradhāna*.
It is called *pradhāna* because everything is deposited (*dhīyate*) or cast (*kṣipyate*) into it pre-eminently (*prakṛṣṭam*).
Here it is asked: "There is no need for a subtle body;
in that case, how is it that the thirteenfold instrument (*karaṇa*) itself transmigrates? To this it is replied:
"Just as a painting cannot exist without a support, and just as a shadow cannot exist without a post or the like,"
In the same way, the subtle body (liṅga) does not remain without its specific attributes (viśeṣas), for it cannot exist without a substratum.
In this case, a relationship between a substratum and that which is supported by it is observed;
for that which is supported does not remain without a substratum. A painting remains by taking a wall or a cloth as its substratum.
This subtle body, which serves as the support for the wall or canvas and the locus for the painting, is the thirteenfold instrument (*karaṇa*).
This being so, your statement that it is the thirteenfold instrument alone that transmigrates is false.
Furthermore: "Just as there is no shadow without a post or similar object."
Just as a shadow does not exist without a post, a person, or the like,
and those [objects] do not exist without the shadow;
and just as light does not exist without fire.
In the same way, the subtle body (*liṅga*) does not remain without a support; it does not exist without the *aviśeṣas*.

The *aviśeṣas* are the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), which—like milk or water in their natural state—are devoid of the qualities of being peaceful, terrible, or deluded. The subtle body is that which is composed of these.
Without that subtle body initiated at the beginning of creation, the subtle body known as the thirteenfold instrument cannot remain without a support.
Therefore, what you have stated— that "what is the use of postulating a subtle body composed of non-specific elements, since it is the thirteenfold instrument itself that transmigrates?"—
is false.

Here it is asked: by what cause does the subtle body, endowed with the thirteenfold instruments, transmigrate? To this it is replied: This subtle body (liṅga) functions like an actor, due to the purpose of the Puruṣa, through the connection of causes and their effects, and because of its association with the omnipresence of Prakṛti. (ISk 42)
The primary cause (pradhāna) initiates activity because it thinks, "The purpose of the Spirit (puruṣārtha) must be accomplished.
And that purpose is twofold:
characterized by the perception of sound and so forth, and characterized by the perception of the distinction between the qualities (guṇas) and the Spirit.

The perception of sound and other objects, the attainment of enjoyments in the worlds of Brahmā and elsewhere, and the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa* constitute liberation (*mokṣa*).
Therefore, it has been said: "This subtle body exists for the sake of the purpose of the *puruṣa*.
Furthermore: "By way of the connection between the cause and its effect... (p. 43).
In that context, the sign (*nimitta*) is eightfold, beginning with the dharma; we shall explain this later in the passage beginning, "By means of the dharma, one goes upward.
Primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the primary matter (*pradhāna*).
Mastery (*vibhutva*) means sovereignty; through its connection with that [mastery] (*tadvibhutvayogāt*).

Just as a certain king, by virtue of his sovereignty, does whatever he desires within his own kingdom, so too primordial matter (*pradhāna*), by virtue of its sovereignty, produces either a human, a divine, or an animal state of existence.
Thus, the subtle body, joined with the thirteenfold instrument, enters the womb of a female elephant and becomes an elephant;
entering a woman's body, it becomes a human;
or it becomes an animal.
Therefore, the gender remains fixed like that of an actor.
Here it is asked: It was stated previously that the subtle body (*liṅga*), permeated by dispositions (*bhāva*), transmigrates. What, then, are these dispositions? To this it is replied:
The dispositions are those innate (*sāṃsiddhika*), those derived from primordial nature (*prākṛtika*), and those resulting from modification (*vaikṛta*), such as virtue (*dharma*) and the rest.
The embryo and its subsequent stages are observed to depend both upon the instruments [of action] and upon the effects [of those actions].
Three kinds of states are considered:
among them, some are innate, while others are natural.
Some are produced by transformation (*vaikṛta*).

Among these, first are those that are innate (*sāṃsiddhika*): for example, when the venerable Kapila, the supreme seer, was born at the beginning of creation, these four dispositions—dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—were produced simultaneously with him.
These are called the *sāṃsiddhikas*.
It is said that there were the sons of Brahmā known as the Prākṛtikas, namely Sanaka and the others.

For these four types of dispositions, which arose spontaneously—like the discovery of a treasure—for those embodied beings who had already produced their bodies and organs at the age of sixteen, they appeared all at once.
And these are called natural states (*prākṛtika*). As for the modified states (*vaikṛtika*): those produced with reference to the form of the teacher and so forth are called modified.
Knowledge arises having made the teacher the instrumental cause (*nimitta*).
From knowledge comes dispassion; from dispassion, dharma; from dharma, sovereignty.
Thus, these four dispositions exist even in ourselves and others;
they alone are called the "transformed" (*vaikṛta*).
